Name: ORZID NE GMENU ABX ABSCESS MORE
Description: This is a page with additional information about management of abscesses. Created 21-Mar-03.  Greg Filice

Contents.Text: Obtain material for Gram stain and culture whenever possible.
Always order "Culture & Susceptibility" and "Anaerobe Culture" under Routine
Order "AFB Culture" or "Mycology Culture" when clinical circumstances suggest
Likely pathogens can be predicted by the site of the abscess, circumstances that
resulted in the abscess, and the gram stain.  Antimicrobials should be active
Most abscesses should be drained.  Involvement of the relevant surgical service
in evaluation and management is strongly recommended.
Cases must be individualized depending on location of the abscess, adequacy of
drainage, host defenses, and the clinical response.  There are no firm rules.
Minor superficial abscesses may respond to incision and drainage and not need
antimicrobials.  For difficult cases, antimicrobials may need to be given
intravenously for many days or weeks.

DisplayText: About this antimicrobial decision support system

Contents.Text: ABOUT THIS ANTIMICROBIAL DECISION SUPPORT SYSTEM
Improve outcomes and reduce antimicrobial resistance
Optimal antimicrobial selection can be complicated and difficult.  Improve-
ments will lead to better outcomes for your patient, fewer adverse effects, and
reduced antimicrobial resistance in your patient and the hospital environment.
This system has been developed locally with input from a broad and representa-
tive group of clinicians.  Recommendations have been based on local suscepti-
bility patterns, clinical evidence, local preferences, and national guidelines.
When recommended antimicrobials are chosen, approval by infectious disease or
other services will not be necessary.  The system allows selection of alter-
native drugs when the recommended drugs are contraindicated. The clinician must
provide a reason for the alternative drug.
Select a diagnosis or condition from the initial menu.
The next page will offer guidelines and 1 or more recommended choices.
Click on the choice that fits your patient the best.
The system offers help in several sections.

infections are usually not severe.  Enterococci are an important cause of
endocarditis that is difficult to treat successfully.  Enterococci are
frequently present in mixed infections, but they often have a minor role in
pathogenesis.  In mixed infections, therapy directed against other, more
virulent pathogens present at the site is usually sufficient.
Susceptibilities for enterococcus species are difficult to interpret.  The
microbiology laboratory reports susceptibility to drugs commonly used for
enterococcal infections.  More information may be available by telephone,

S. aureus is a major human pathogen.  It lives on skin and mucus membranes in
approximately 40% of people, most commonly in the anterior nares.  S. aureus is
frequently involved in abscesses or endovascular infections, including
endocarditis, and these diseases often relapse.
For deep seated infections, give antimicrobials IV for 4-6 weeks.  If there is
an easily removable or drainable focus (e.g., infected iv catheter, minor
abscess, urinary cystitis, mild-moderate pneumonia), give antimicrobials IV for
Addition of gentamicin  or rifampin to beta lactam drugs or vancomycin enhances
killing in vitro.  Clinical trials have shown that addition of gentamicin
improves symptoms about 1 day faster, but it does not improve outcomes or
prevent complications.  There is no evidence that rifampin improves outcomes.
Addition of either drug will increase the risk of adverse effects.

Renal disease:  history of chronic renal disease or abnormal blood urea nitrogen

Clean:  An uninfected wound without inflammation, and the respiratory,

wound will be closed primarily, and, if necessary, drained with closed

be included in this category if they meet the criteria.
Clean-Contaminated:  The respiratory, alimentary, genital, or urinary tract will
be entered under controlled conditions, without unusual contamination. Opera

cluded provided there is no evidence of infection or major break in technique.

gastrointestinal tract.  Incisions in which acute, non-purulent inflammation
Dirty-Infected:  Old traumatic wounds with retained devitalized tissue and those

Clean:  Antimicrobial prophylaxis (AMP) usually not indicated.  Exceptions

duration of therapy for contaminated wound (e.g., perforated viscus, bite
wound, compound fracture) is for 5 days.
Dirty:  Antimicrobials are therapeutic and not prophylactic.

Contents.Text: LYME DISEASE AND OTHER TICK-BORNE ILLNESSES
Patients who display signs of illness or fever within 30 days of removing an
attached tick should be evaluated for tick-borne illness. In the upper Midwest
these are Lyme, anaplasmosis, babesiosis, ehrlichiosis, and Powassan vir
disease. Patients who have been bitten by an Ixodes spp. tick (deer tick) but
who do not display signs or symptoms of infection should not be treated with
antimicrobials. Refer to recommendations below for pathogen specific
Powassan virus disease - contact Infectious Diseases for more Information.
Lyme disease results from the transmission of Borrelia burgdorferi from an
Ixodes spp. tick bite. Prophylactic antimicrobial treatment may be beneficial in
certain patients who have been bitten while in endemic areas.
Except for erythema migrans, Lyme disease is a complicated, difficult disease to

therapy and treatment duration based on pathogen once isolated.

Contents.Text: COMMUNITY-ACQUIRED PNEUMONIA (CAP) TREATED IN AN INPATIENT SETTING
Be sure of the diagnosis. Careful reviews have shown that over half of
people treated for community-acquired pneumonia do not in fact have
pneumonia. Pneumonia is likely in persons with 3 or more signs or symptoms
including a) new infiltrate (or, no prior film for comparison) b) new
crackles, egophony, or dullness c) pleuritic pain, d) fever and/or chills
e) leukocytosis f) cough g) purulent sputum and h) new or worsened dyspnea
or tachypnea, and no likely alternative explanation for the presentation.
Common alternative explanations include heart failure, thromboembolic
disease, COPD exacerbation, viral pneumonitis, aspiration pneumonitis, or
tumor. Most of the latter conditions do NOT benefit from antimicrobials.
Pharmacological therapy of community-acquired pneumonia in inpatients
should include 1 or 2 antimicrobial(s) and corticosteroids (Siemieniuk, et
al, 2015). Corticosteroid therapy decreases the risk of death, decreases
the need for ventilation and ICU admission, and shortens length of stay.
Corticosteroid therapy is likely to increase blood glucose concentrations
Recommendation for duration of antibiotic therapy for CAP:
Patients with CAP should be treated for a minimum of 5 days, should be
afebrile for 48-72 hours, and should have no more than 1 CAP-
associated sign of clinical instability before discontinuation
Temperature less than/equal to 100 degrees F
Heart rate less than/equal to 100 beats/minute
Respiratory rate less than/equal to 24 breaths/minute
Systolic blood pressure greater than/equal to 90 mm Hg
Arterial oxygen saturation greater than/equal to 90% --OR--
PO2 greater than/equal to 60 mm Hg on room air
Treatment on MEDICAL WARD (not intensive care)
Most patients respond in 3-5 days and treatment should ordinarily last 5-7
days. Risk factors indicating that pseudomonas is a possible cause of
community-acquired pneumonia include severe structural lung disease
(e.g. bronchiectasis), recent antibiotic therapy, or recent stay in a hospital.
If community-associated methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is
suspected (e.g., post influenza, injection drug user,Gram positive cocci in
clusters on Gram stain), add antibiotic to cover MRSA. (see below)
If Pseudomonas is NOT a likely pathogen
If Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a consideration (e.g. chronic or structural
lung disease, recent antibiotic therapy, recent hospitalization)
If community MRSA is suspected (e.g., post-influenza, injection drug user,
Gram positive cocci in clusters on Gram stain) ADD MRSA coverage

Contents.Text: Epididymitis is inflammation of the epididymis and when testicles are involved
is referred to as epididymo-orchitis. Acute epididymitis is the most common
cause of scrotal pain in adults. Other features include scrotal erythema and
edema, pyuria, dysuria, thickened epididymis, swollen testis, and is usually
unilateral. It is primarily caused by infection but can also result from trauma
and autoimmune diseases. Testicular torsion should be ruled out before
treatment. Most cases in men aged 35 and older, those with recent urinary tract
instrumentation or surgery (e.g., prostate biopsy, vasectomy) are associated
with enteric Gram-negative rods. Most cases in men under age 35 are associated
with N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Resistant organisms are more likely if
the patient has been in the hospital for more than 48 hours or received a course
of antibiotics. There is increasing resistance in urinary pathogens to
A urine analysis, urine culture and urine nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT)
should be performed in all cases of suspected epididymitis before starting
Patients at risk of sexually transmitted infections should be assessed for
treatment. Refer to the Urogenital section of the Antimicrobial CDSS for more
Patients with bacterial epididymitis treated with antibiotics should improve
within two or three days. If no improvement is noted, other causes of scrotal
pain and referral to a urologist should be considered.
Management should include bed rest, analgesics, and scrotal elevation. Older men
should have their residual urinary volume checked. If the residual volume is
elevated, the patient should be seen by a urologist as epididymitis is unlikely
to respond if the prostate is blocking the vas deferens.

Contents.Text: Epididymitis is inflammation of the epididymis and when testicles are involved
is referred to as epididymo-orchitis. Acute epididymitis is the most common
cause of scrotal pain in adults. Other features include scrotal erythema and
edema, pyuria, dysuria, thickened epididymis, swollen testis, and is usually
unilateral. It is primarily caused by infection but can also result from trauma
and autoimmune diseases. Testicular torsion should be ruled out before
treatment. Most cases in men aged 35 and older, those with recent urinary tract
instrumentation or surgery (e.g., prostate biopsy, vasectomy) are associated
with enteric Gram-negative rods. Most cases in men under age 35 are associated
with N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Resistant organisms are more likely if
the patient has been in the hospital for more than 48 hours or received a course
of antibiotics. There is increasing resistance in urinary pathogens to
A urine analysis, urine culture and urine nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT)
should be performed in all cases of suspected epididymitis before starting
Patients at risk of sexually transmitted infections should be assessed for
treatment. Refer to the Urogenital section of the Antimicrobial CDSS for more
Patients with bacterial epididymitis treated with antibiotics should improve
within two or three days. If no improvement is noted, other causes of scrotal
pain and referral to a urologist should be considered.
Management should include bed rest, analgesics, and scrotal elevation. Older men
should have their residual urinary volume checked. If the residual volume is
elevated, the patient should be seen by a urologist as epididymitis is unlikely
to respond if the prostate is blocking the vas deferens.

The risk of severe, rapidly progressive infections increases when the absolute
neutrophil count (ANC, segmented neutrophils plus bands) is less than 500
cells/microliter. The risk increases dramatically when the ANC is <100
cells/microliter. Because of these risks, patients with fever and neutropenia to
this degree should receive empirical antimicrobial therapy immediately.
Empirical therapy should also be given to patients with fever and ANC 500-1000
cells/microliter when the concentration is expected to be <500 cells/microliter
within the next 48 hours. For this purpose, fever is defined as a single
Since infection can be rapidly progressive and severe, broad-spectrum
antimicrobials are given urgently to patients with neutropenic fever as defined
above. Vancomycin should only be given when there are clear indications for its
Candidates for empirical treatment with oral antimicrobials include those who
are febrile but who have no evidence of focal infection or signs or symptoms of
severe disease, like hypotension. Outpatient antimicrobials for neutropenic

Contents.Text: Features of pyelonephritis include fever/other signs of systemic infection,
flank pain, costovertebral tenderness, and pelvic or perianal pain in men. Most
cases are caused by Escherichia coli. Resistant organisms, such as Enterococcus
and Pseudomonas, are more likely if the patient is elderly, has been in the
hospital for more than 48 hours, or received a course of antibiotics.
Obtain a urine culture with  Gram-stain, and blood cultures 2 sets 15 min apart
immediately to guide antimicrobial therapy. Broad spectrum antimicrobials are
needed if patient is at risk of having a multi-drug resistant (MDR) organism.
Oral regimens are preferred over IV if severity is mild or moderate and patient
can tolerate oral antibiotics. In patients with severe or persistent disease,
new renal failure, or suspected urinary obstruction, obtain a renal ultrasound
to rule out obstruction or other complicating condition. Consult urology if
When patients who require parenteral therapy are afebrile, clinically stable,
and can take oral medication, convert to oral therapy based on the
identification and susceptibility of the isolate.

Contents.Text: Per the Sepsis-3 task force, sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ
dysfunction caused by dysregulated host response to infection.
Septic shock is a subset of sepsis in which profound circulatory, cellular, and
metabolic abnormalities occur. Septic shock requires vasopressor therapy and is
associated with in-hospital mortality greater than 40%.
Early intervention is crucial to prevention of death from sepsis. Antimicrobials
active against likely pathogens, based on source infection, and supportive
treatment to maintain vascular perfusion should be initiated immediately (within
the first hour of patient presentation). Reassess antimicrobial therapy daily to
narrow therapeutic spectrum when culture and susceptibility data are available.

quick orders pre-programmed with appropriate antimicrobial regimens for specific
Improve patient outcomes, reduce rates of microbial resistance, prevent adverse

shown significant improvement in appropriate use of antimicrobials when CDSS
The Minneapolis VAHCS has a restricted antimicrobial formulary. A restricted

Contents.Text: Acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) typically presents with fever, dysuria,
chills, malaise, myalgia, pelvic or perianal pain. On exam, the prostate gland
is tense, boggy, and extremely tender. The urinalysis reveals pyuria, and the
urine culture is positive. Men with dysuria and fever but without pyuria and/or
bacteriuria should be seen by a urologist. If there is any suspicion of abscess,
the patient should be seen by a urologist.
Those with recent urinary tract instrumentation or surgery (e.g., prostate
biopsy, vasectomy) are associated with enteric Gram-negative rods. There are
cases of ABP associated with N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Resistant
organisms are more likely if the patient has been in the hospital for more than
48 hours or received a course of antibiotics. There is increasing resistance in
A midstream urine sample before antibiotics are taken and send for culture and
susceptibility testing should be performed in all patients to guide
antimicrobial therapy. When S. aureus is recovered from a urine
culture, it is important to perform blood cultures to evaluate whether the
bacteriuria reflects seeding of the prostate or urine from bacteremia.
Patients at risk of sexually transmitted infections should be assessed for
Duration of therapy for ABP is usually 2 weeks, although it can be continued for
up to 4 weeks for severe illness or treatment of patients with concomitant
Give oral antibiotics first line if the person can take oral medicines, and the
severity of their condition does not require intravenous antibiotics.

Contents.Text: E. Coli, Pseudomonas, or another organism
Meningitis is an inflammation of the meninges and tissues surrounding the brain
and spinal cord. It is characterized by an abnormal amount of white blood cells
in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and symptoms include headache, fever, mental
status changes, nuchal rigidity, and nausea.
The sudden onset of meningeal symptoms within hours to days caused by several
infectious etiologies, including bacterial, viral, fungal and protozoa, as well
as non-infectious etiologies. Bacterial meningitis is the most common type of
meningitis, accounting for up to 90% of cases where a CSF culture was obtained
prior to starting antimicrobials. Non-bacterial meningitis is commonly referred
to as aseptic meningitis (refer to "Negative CSF culture" below for
Patients with acute bacterial meningitis often have severe symptoms and present
soon after onset of infection. The relationship between predisposing factors and
common bacterial pathogen are listed below.
Predisposing Factors and Common Bacterial Pathogens
*Age > 50 years - S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, L. monocytogenes, aerobic
*Immunocompromised state - S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, L. monocytogenes,
*Basilar skull fracture - S. pneumoniae: H. influenzae, group A and
*Head trauma: after neurosurgery - Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase-negative
Initial Management of Suspected Acute Bacterial Meningitis
Once a diagnosis of acute bacterial meningitis is considered likely,
antimicrobials should be initiated as soon as possible. Two blood cultures
should be drawn. Lumbar puncture (LP) should be performed in nearly all patients
to obtain CSF for establishing diagnosis and determining infectious
organism/susceptibility. Computed tomography (CT) should be performed prior to
LP in some patients (see list below). If CT must be obtained prior to LP or
there is another delay in performing LP, empiric antimicrobials should not be
delayed and initiated immediately after obtaining blood cultures only.
Relative LP contraindications (no absolute contraindications exist):
Anticoagulation therapy or bleeding disorder, spinal epidural abscess, raised
Computed tomography scan should be performed prior to lumbar puncture in cases
with the following: Immunocompromise, history of CNS disease, new onset seizure,
papilledema, abnormal level of consciousness, focal neurologic deficit.
LP opening pressure is often elevated in bacterial meningitis. CSF findings
characteristic of bacterial meningitis include CSF glucose <40mg/dL, CSF to
serum glucose ratio </=0.4, CSF protein concentration >/=200 mg/dL and CSF WBC
Empiric Treatment After Blood Cultures are Drawn, and CSF is Obtained, or if LP
Empiric Treatment Based on CSF Gram-Stain Results
When gram stain results are available, adjust antimicrobials to optimize therapy
Treatment Based on CSF Isolated Organism
When infectious organism is identified, adjust antimicrobials to optimize therap
Patients who have a negative CSF culture but have symptoms and CSF findings
consistent with bacterial meningitis should be treated based on likely pathogen.
Patients with negative CSF culture, symptoms of acute meningitis but have labs
inconsistent with bacterial meningitis should be considered to have aseptic
meningitis. Aseptic meningitis is caused by a variety of non-bacterial
infectious etiologies and non-infectious etiologies. Consult Infectious Disease

BRONCHITIS, NO BENEFIT FROM ANTIBACTERIAL THERAPY
Acute bronchitis is a clinical syndrome with a brief, self-limited pneumonia on
chest radiograph. It is accompanied by dry or productive cough lasting up to 3
weeks, is most prevalent in winter, and is primarily caused by viruses. More
than 1 in 20 people have acute bronchitis per year, with highest rates during
the winter months.  This discussion does not pertain to acute exacerbations of
chronic bronchitis, a clinical syndrome also frequently associated with viral
infection, but in which bacteria play a more important role.
Narcotic cough suppressants, expectorants, antihistamines, decongestants, and
beta 2-agonists have been used to treat patients with acute bronchitis, but
controlled trials have not clearly concluded that they are beneficial.
Empirical antibacterial therapy has repeatedly been shown to provide no benefit
for most patients.  Acute bronchitis remains one of the five most frequently
cited rationales for excessive antibiotic use in outpatients. Acute bronchitis
and other acute respiratory syndromes (otitis media, sinusitis, pharyngitis,
upper respiratory infections) account for approximately 75% of ambulatory
prescriptions in the United States.  Current guidelines, endorsed by several
national societies, including the Infectious Diseases Society of America, do not
recommend the routine use of antibiotics for uncomplicated acute bronchitis in
If pertussis is suspected, early therapy with macrolides or tetracyclines is
indicated to prevent transmission, although the clinical findings early in
pertussis infection are indistinguishable from viral causes of bronchitis, and
the incidence of disease is very low.  Treat for pertussis only when a patient
has likely been exposed to other cases.

For patients who have recently been treated for cervicitis

transmitted infection. If diagnostic tests for the cause of cervicitis are not
feasible, therapy for both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis should be given to

CHRONIC PROSTATITIS / CHRONIC PELVIC PAIN SYNDROME
Chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CP/CPPS) is a clinical
syndrome in males defined by pain or discomfort in the pelvic region, often
accompanied by urologic symptoms or sexual dysfunction. Despite the use of the
term "prostatitis," it is unclear to what degree the prostate is the source of
Research guidelines define chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome
(CP/CPPS) as chronic pelvic pain for at least three of the preceding six months
in the absence of other identifiable causes, often associated with urinary
This syndrome presents with intermittent perineal and/or low back pain,
obstructive voiding symptoms, relatively normal examination, and negative urine
cultures. In patients who have a negative urine culture and features consistent
with CP/CPPS, antimicrobial therapy is not indicated.
Consult urology for non-antimicrobial therapy recommendations (e.g. alpha-
adrenergic antagonists, anti-inflammatory medications) to reduce symptoms.

Contents.Text: COLONIZED RESPIRATORY TRACT IN A PATIENT ON A VENTILATOR
The respiratory tracts of persons who are intubated, have a
tracheostomy, or have other abnormalities of the larynx or trachea are
usually colonized with bacteria and often fungi. The bacteria can be of
relatively low virulence (e.g. coagulase negative staphylococci, streptococci,
candida) or of potentially greater virulence (Staphylococcus aureus,
enterobacteriaceae, pseudomonas). Candida and enterococci are common
respiratory tract colonizers and they almost never cause pneumonia. There is
no benefit from treatment of patients with systemic antimicrobials simply
because the respiratory tract is colonized with a potential pathogen and there
is no evidence of an infiltrate. Systemic antimicrobial therapy will select for
resistant organisms and may lead to other adverse effects.
See below for ventilator-associated pneumonia treatment recommendations in

Contents.Text: Open wounds are usually colonized with bacteria and often fungi. This is true of
ulcers (see below), post-operative wounds, traumatic wounds, and others. Then
bacteria can be of relatively low virulence (eg, coagulase negative
staphylococci, diphtheroids) or of potentially greater virulence (Staphylococcus
aureus, enterobacteriaceae, pseudomonas). Candida is commonly present on wounds
that are moist or covered. There is no need to treat patients with systemic
antimicrobials simply because a wound culture is positive for a potential
pathogen. Topical antimicrobials are not effective in nearly all circumstances
and can select for resistant organisms or lead to other adverse effects.
Systemic antimicrobial therapy may be indicated if there are signs of infection.

Signs and symptoms that may indicate infection has extended beyond the bladder

Contents.Text: Diagnosis and management are complex. Cardiology, Infectious Disease, and
Surgery services should all be involved in diagnosis and management of infective
Endocarditis is the result of growth of microorganisms on endothelium of the
heart. The integrity of the endothelial surface must be compromised in order to
allow microorganisms to attach and proliferate. Often such lesions are caused by
abnormal blood flow or thrombi resulting from heart valvular disease, prosthetic
heart valves, or from foreign material or microorganisms introduced to the
bloodstream as byproducts of illicit intravenous drug use.
Endocarditis should be considered a possible diagnosis in a patient with
persistent bacteremia without an identifiable focal infection, especially when
the patient has a structural heart abnormality, prosthesis, or has a recent
history of intravenous illicit drug use.
Diagnosis of endocarditis can be based on several combinations of signs and
symptoms. The Duke criteria help categorize cases as definite or possible
endocarditis based on major and minor criteria. The Duke criteria also indicate
when a diagnosis of endocarditis can be excluded.
Endocarditis is categorized by time course and severity of symptoms of illness
into acute and subacute. These classifications help suggest which pathogens may
be more likely associated with symptoms.
Acute endocarditis is a rapidly progressing illness that often causes fever. It
can be associated with spread of infection to other parts of the body and can
cause death within a matter of weeks. In patient with suspected acute
endocarditis, three sets of blood cultures should be obtained with the first and
last cultures separated by at least one hour. Empiric antimicrobial therapy
should then be initiated as soon as possible.
Subacute endocarditis follows an indolent course. Generally, patients have had
some symptoms for at least 2 weeks. Symptoms are more subtle and spread of
infection to other systems is uncommon. In patients with suspected subacute
endocarditis, every attempt should be made to identify a pathogen prior to
initiating antimicrobial therapy. These patients should be observed carefully
for signs of heart failure or embolic complications, and if signs are noted,

neutropenia. They are caused by antibody (usually IgG)- mediated cell
2) Type III reactions can manifest as serum sickness, vasculitis or Arthus
reaction, and are caused by IgG:drug immune complex deposition and complement
3) Type IV reactions typically manifest as contact dermatitis, morbilliform
epidermal necrolysis) and other presentations. They are T-cell mediated.
Repeated exposures lead to reactions that are of the same type.
Approximately 10% of patients report a beta-lactam allergy. Up to 90% of these
patients can tolerate penicillin and have been designated penicillin allergic
unnecessarily. Patients allergic to cephalosporins will have a cross-reaction to
penicillins 3% to 5% of the time. Overall, patients with a history of penicillin
allergy can tolerate cephalosporins although there are rare reports to severe,
sometimes fatal anaphylactic reactions. Neither penicillin- or cephalosporin-
allergic patients will react to aztreonam. The degree of cross-reactivity of
penicillins and cephalosporins with carbapenems appears to be low.
If a patient has had an immediate reaction to a drug in the past, an allergy
specialist should evaluate the patient before a drug of the same class is
administered to the patient. Patients with delayed onset reactions causing
fever, systemic symptoms or mucosal involvement should also be evaluated by an
allergy specialist before a drug of the same class is administered.
A patient with previous Type I reaction to a beta-lactam can be desensitized and
then receive therapeutic doses of the same class within a day. Severe
reactions during desensitization are uncommon. Pharmacy service must be

In most cases, if a person is suspected of having been exposed to influenza,

The provider should explain the early signs and symptoms of influenza to the

resident or staff with influenza-like illness.

Epididymitis is inflammation of the epididymis and when testicles are involved
is referred to as epididymo-orchitis. Acute epididymitis is the most common
cause of scrotal pain in adults. Other features include scrotal erythema and
edema, pyuria, dysuria, thickened epididymis, swollen testis, and is usually
unilateral. It is primarily caused by infection but can also result from trauma
and autoimmune diseases. Testicular torsion should be ruled out before
treatment. Most cases in men aged 35 and older, those with recent urinary tract
instrumentation or surgery (e.g., prostate biopsy, vasectomy) are associated
with enteric Gram-negative rods. Most cases in men under age 35 are associated
with N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Resistant organisms are more likely if
the patient has been in the hospital for more than 48 hours or received a course
of antibiotics. There is increasing resistance in urinary pathogens to
A urine analysis, urine culture and urine nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT)
should be performed in all cases of suspected epididymitis before starting
Patients at risk of sexually transmitted infections should be assessed for

Patients with bacterial epididymitis treated with antibiotics should improve
within two or three days. If no improvement is noted, other causes of scrotal
pain and referral to a urologist should be considered.
Management should include bed rest, analgesics, and scrotal elevation. Older men
should have their residual urinary volume checked. If the residual volume is
elevated, the patient should be seen by a urologist as epididymitis is unlikely
to respond if the prostate is blocking the vas deferens.

lactamases, AmpC beta-lactamases and oxacillinases. These enzymes are most
common in strains of Acinetobacter, Citrobacter, Enterobacter, Escherichia coli,
Klebsiella, Proteus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Salmonella, and Serratia
marcescens. The enzymes can be latent under many circumstances. However, in
patients receiving beta lactam antibiotics, the enzymes can be expressed and
contribute to treatment failure. Because of this, and since the enzymes continue
to evolve, they are difficult to detect in clinical microbiology laboratories.
Bacteria carrying these enzymes are often also resistant to many other commonly
used antimicrobials, including trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, quinolones, and
others, through different mechanisms. Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas and
Acinetobacter are increasingly resistant to all antimicrobials.
Clinicians must be aware that these enzymes may not be detected in all strains
that carry them. If a Gram-negative infection is not responding to therapy with
a beta lactam drug, consider adding or switching to a drug that is not a beta
lactam and appears active in the susceptibility report.
If a patient is suspected of having a Gram-negative infection and is likely to
be colonized with bacteria carrying these enzymes, empirical therapy with
alternative drugs that are not inactivated by them should be considered.

Ocular herpes infection can be caused by either HSV-1 or HSV-2. The majority of
cases are caused by HSV-1. The recurrence rate of ocular herpes is 40% over a 5
year period, less than that of oral or genital herpes. Ocular herpes is a
major cause of blindness and typically presents as infection of the epithelium
of the cornea but can also rarely involve the stroma and endothelium.
Involvement of the stroma or endothelium requires treatment with topical
steroid and close monitoring. For these cases, start oral antiviral and consult
Antiviral prophylaxis is recommended for patients with multiple recurrences,
recurrent episodes with ulceration, recurrent inflammation with
scar/vascularization approaching visual axis, patients who have had keratoplasty
for HSV-related scarring/astigmatism, and patients who have had HSV keratitis
while on immunosuppressive therapy. Post-surgical prophylaxis is not discussed
here. Please consult ophthalmology for more information.

Contents.Text: HOW TO FIND AN ALTERNATIVE ANTIMICROBIAL WITHIN THE CDSS
The CDSS has been developed locally with input from a broad, representative
group of clinicians. All antimicrobial recommendations within the Antimicrobial
CDSS are reviewed by a clinical pharmacist and an Infectious Diseases Medical
Specialist. Recommendations provided are based on local susceptibility patterns,
clinical evidence, local preferences, and national guidelines. In rare cases,
the recommended antimicrobials and listed alternatives may not be preferred for
the patient you are treating (e.g. isolate resistance, allergies, etc.). In
these cases, a broader set of alternative antimicrobials may be ordered through
the Antimicrobial CDSS. Like other antimicrobial orders in the CDSS,
antimicrobials ordered through the Alternative Antimicrobials menu do on require
a prior authorization or ID approval.
To access the Alternative Antimicrobials menu, navigate to the menu containing
antimicrobial recommendations for the infectious disease you are treating. At
the top of the menu, select the option Need an alternative antimicrobial
(typically item #6). Select the reason an alternative antimicrobial is required,
then the Alternative Antimicrobials menu will pop up.
The Alternative Antimicrobial menu contains antimicrobial regimens that have
been deemed appropriate for use as alternatives to recommended antimicrobials by
the Antimicrobial P&T Subcommittee. If the list does not contain the preferred
antimicrobial, contact or consult Infectious Diseases.
The regimens provided in the Alternative Antimicrobial menu are not tailored for
a specific infectious disease. The dose, frequency, and duration must be changed
based on the infectious disease you are treating as well as for patient specific
factors. The usage of alternative antimicrobials are monitored by the
Antimicrobial CDSS team for appropriateness and to identify infectious diseases

Contents.Text: How to find an alternative antimicrobial within the CDSS
The CDSS has been designed to offer antimicrobial prescribing advice quickly and
efficiently. Since inpatient and outpatient drugs are ordered differently, the
CDSS has both and inpatient and outpatient versions for prescribing.
The Antimicrobial CDSS is located within CPRS. When CPRS is open, click on the
Orders tab at the bottom left hand side of the CPRS window.
On the left-hand side of the Orders tab, click on the Medicine Inpt Orders.
On the left-hand side of the Orders tab, click on the Medicine Outpt Orders.
The main menu of the Antimicrobial CDSS contains links to categories of
infectious diseases based on syndrome/organ system (e.g. cardiovascular,
genitourinary, etc.), organisms (e.g. gram-positive bacteria, gram-negative
bacteria, viruses, etc.) and other special cases. To navigate to specific
infectious disease, select the category the infectious disease is associated
with. Within the category menu, select the specific infectious disease sub-menu
for recommendations, quick orders and pertinent resources (e.g., section-
specific consults, important drug properties, CDSS system help resources, etc.).
The Index is in the main menu at the top of the left-hand column under the
header Index of Antimicrobial CDSS content. The Index contains an alphabetized
list of Antimicrobial CDSS content. Find the infectious disease, organism or
other topic you are looking for by scrolling down the list. When you locate the
term you are looking for, click on it to be linked to the menu containing
specific recommendations, quick orders and pertinent resources.
Quick orders are preprogrammed with the usually recommended antimicrobial dose,
frequency and solution for the specific infectious disease.
Quick orders are not tailored to specific patient factors such as renal
insufficiency, comorbidities, contraindications, weight, allergies, etc. The
provider must assess every patient closely for these factors and modify
recommended antimicrobials if needed. To assist the provider, additional drug
information is provided within specific infectious diseases recommendation menus
and a link to more in depth information is provided at the top of these menus.

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) type 1 is the leading cause of sporadic fatal
encephalitis worldwide and should be suspected in patients who have symptoms
unexplained by other causes. Typical symptoms include acute alteration of
consciousness for more than 24 hours, fever, new onset seizures and/or focal
neurologic deficits. Patients taking natalizumab are at increased risk of HSV
encephalitis. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential to achieve resolution
of infection and symptoms. If diagnosis is not certain and there is little
likelihood of herniation, obtain cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample for HSV
polymerase chain reaction (PCR). MRI without contrast nearly always show
abnormal signs in patients with HSV encephalitis. Neurology and Infectious
Treatment, Initiate Immediately When HSV Encephalitis is Suspected

Contents.Text: Impetigo is a superficial skin infection that rarely causes systemic
symptoms. Ecthyma is a skin infection characterized by crusted sores
beneath which ulcers form. It is a deep form of impetigo, as the same
bacteria causing the infection are involved. Ecthyma causes deeper
erosions of the skin into the dermis.
Gram stain and culture of the pus or exudates from skin lesions of
impetigo and ecthyma are recommended to help identify whether
Staphylococcus aureus and/or beta-hemolytic Streptococcus is the cause.
Bullous and non-bullous impetigo can be treated with oral or topical
antimicrobials, but oral therapy is recommended for patients with
numerous lesions or in outbreaks affecting several people to help

Contents.Text: LYME DISEASE AND OTHER TICK-BORNE ILLNESSES
Patients who display signs of illness or fever within 30 days of removing an
attached tick should be evaluated for tick-borne illness. In the upper Midwest
these are Lyme, anaplasmosis, babesiosis, ehrlichiosis, and Powassan virus
disease. Patients who have been bitten by an Ixodes spp. tick (deer tick) but
who do not display signs or symptoms of infection should not be treated with
antimicrobials. Refer to recommendations below for pathogen specific
Powassan virus disease - contact Infectious Diseases for more Information.
Lyme disease results from the transmission of Borrelia burgdorferi from an
Ixodes spp. tick bite. Prophylactic antimicrobial treatment may be beneficial in
certain patients who have been bitten while in endemic areas.
Except for erythema migrans, Lyme disease is a complicated, difficult disease to
diagnose and treat. Infectious Diseases consultation is strongly encouraged.

ambulatory visits in the United States.  The major treatable pathogen, group
A streptococcus (GAS), is the cause of pharyngitis in only approximately 10
percent of adults who seek medical care.  The vast majority of patients
receive presumptive antibiotic therapy for pharyngitis which in most cases is
unnecessary and results in adverse effects including death, increases costs,
and adds to pressure on antimicrobial resistance.  Typical causes of
pharyngitis include viruses in about �, beta-hemolytic streptococci other
than group A in 18%, Mycoplasma pneumoniae in 10%, Chlamydophila pneumoniae
in 8%, Group A streptococci in 5%, and no microbe identified in 1/3.
Rheumatic fever is rare in the United States, especially in adults, so
that some authorities recommend no treatment even if GAS is a potential cause
of pharyngitis.Others feel it is important to detect GAS  since antibiotic
therapy can slightly shorten the acute illness, prevent acute rheumatic fever
and possibly prevent suppurative sequelae.  Other potential causes of
pharyngitis that should be considered and diagnosed if likely include
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) mononucleosis, primary HIV infection, influenza,
gonococcal pharyngitis, diphtheria, and suppurative pharyngeal infections.
The Centor criteria are used to predict whether GAS pharyngitis is present.
If three or four of these criteria are met, the positive predictive value is
40 to 60 percent.  If fewer than three criteria are present, the likelihood
GAS is causing pharyngitis is less than 20 percent.  If 3 or > Centor criteria
are met, obtain a throat culture for group A streptococcus.  Treat
empirically for GAS if the patient has severe symptoms or treat later for GAS
if the throat culture is positive.

Contents.Text: Treatment of Candida Urinary Tract Infections
Asymptomatic bacteriuria (>= 100,000 bacteria per ml of urine) is common in
middle aged and older people, especially those who have chronic medical
conditions. Pyuria is common in persons with bacteriuria and individuals with
indwelling catheters in place. By itself, the presence of pyuria is not
sufficient to diagnose bacteriuria, and the presence or absence of pyuria does
not differentiate symptomatic from asymptomatic urinary infection. Candiduria is
less common than bacteriuria, but the implications of candiduria are similar to
Many studies, including randomized clinical trials have shown that
treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria and candiduria, with or without pyuria is
of no benefit, except in certain well-defined circumstances. Antimicrobial
therapy is always accompanied by risk of harms, including drug reactions,
Clostridium difficile colitis, anaphylaxis and death. Except in circumstances
specified below, it is best to not order urinalysis or urine culture in
asymptomatic persons. If bacteriuria, candiduria or pyuria is discovered in an
asymptomatic person for some reason, antimicrobial therapy should not be given

CONDITIONS NOT BENEFITTED BY ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY
Several common conditions associated with inflammation or
microorganisms do not benefit from antibiotic therapy in most or all cases.
Yet, antimicrobials are frequently prescribed for these conditions leading to
unnecessary toxicity and costs, rare deaths, and the relentless increase in
antimicrobial resistance. Please review these conditions and do not give
antimicrobials for these conditions unless there are extraordinary
circumstances that make your situation different. If you have any questions,
please contact the infectious disease physician on call.

Suppurative Parotitis. Acute bacterial parotitis affects primarily elderly,
malnourished, dehydrated or post-operative patients. Symptoms include fever,
toxicity, and tender swelling along the mandible with purulent drainage from the
parotid duct. Suppurative parotitis is usually unilateral whereas viral
parotitis is usually bilateral. Pain is intense and aggressive, analgesic
therapy is required. Progression of infection may lead to massive swelling of
the neck, respiratory obstruction, septicemia and osteomyelitis of adjacent
facial bones. Empiric antibiotics are required for coverage of Staphylococcus
aureus if bacterial, and surgical drainage is usually necessary.
Chronic Parotitis. Parotitis is recurrent with intermittent acute exacerbations.
Chronic, low-grade bacterial infection results in functional destruction of the
salivary gland. It may be confused with Sjogren's syndrome, a noninfectious
illness. Therapy includes systemic antibiotics. Parotidectomy may eventually be
required for patients with long-standing infection.
Viral Parotitis. Mumps parotitis is characterized by the rapid, painful swelling
of one or both parotid glands within 2 to 3 weeks after exposure to the mumps
virus. Mumps usually involves both parotid glands whereas bacterial parotitis is
unilateral. Other viral causes of parotitis include influenza and enteroviruses.
Mumps parotitis usually resolves spontaneously in 5 to 10 days. Provide

Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) refers to bacterial infection of the upper
female reproductive tract.  Likely bacterial pathogens include Neisseria
gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, anaerobes, enteric Gram-negative rods, and
Streptococcus agalactiae.  PID should be considered in sexually active women
with pelvic tenderness and signs of lower genital tract inflammation.  Signs and
symptoms may be mild or non-specific, and providers should have a low threshold
to initiate treatment. All women who are diagnosed with acute PID should be
tested for N. gonorrohoeae, C. trachomatis, and HIV. Male sex partners of
patients with PID should be examined and treated (see below) if they had sexual
contact within the 60 days before onset of the patient's symptoms.
Judge severity of infection based on clinical signs and symptoms, including

Contents.Text: Treatment of CNS Infected Intravascular Catheters
BLOOD CULTURE POSITIVE FOR COAGULASE NEGATIVE STAPHYLOCOCCI (CNS)
CNS are the most common contaminants isolated from blood cultures. When CNS
isolated from blood cultures represent true bacteremia, the blood is usually
obtained from a patient with plastic or metal in the body. The most common
source of coagulase negative staphylococcal bacteremia is an infected
When CNS are isolated from blood, the physician should carefully assess the
patient to decide whether the isolation represents disease or colonization.
Colonization is more likely if a single bottle is positive or both bottles from
a single blood draw are positive. If multiple bottles are positive from separate
blood draws, it is more likely that the isolates reflect disease or colonization
of an intravascular device. Isolates from contaminated bottles often take
several days to become positive. If the patient has risk factors for true
coagulase negative staphylococcal bacteremia, catheter-related blood stream
infection and/or the patient is severely ill, antimicrobials should be given
(see below). If there is a plastic or metal prosthesis in the body, the
physician should evaluate the site for possible infection. If the isolates are
likely to represent contamination and the patient does not seem ill with CNS,
antimicrobial therapy would not be helpful and should not be given.

Vaccinate all adults greater than or equal to 50 years of age with the

Give recombinant zoster vaccine x2, 2nd dose 2-6 months after the first
Treatment is not beneficial, none is recommended.
Treatment with antivirals can shorten duration of pain and rash in patients over
50 years old. Treatment must be started within 72 hours of onset.
There is evidence that addition of corticosteroids to antiviral
therapy decreases pain and duration of rash and improves quality of life
modestly during the acute shingles episode. Corticosteroids do not decrease the
incidence of post-herpetic neuralgia. Some authorities recommend addition of
corticosteroid therapy to antiviral therapy for patients over age 50 years.
Corticosteroids are not recommended for patients at greater risk for steroid

ulcer disease) or for immunocompromised patients.
Immunocompromised patients at increased risk for complications of VZV disease
include: patients with malignancy, current immunosuppressive therapy, or HIV
infection. Treatment with antivirals shortens duration of symptoms and reduces
incidence of complications. In immunocompromised patients, treatment is
recommended to be started at any point during an active infection.

Contents.Text: Functional or Anatomical Asplenia Vaccine & Antibiotic Prophylaxis Guideline
Following a splenectomy there is considerably increased risk of developing
septicemia from invasive encapsulated organisms, namely Streptococcus pneumonia,
Haemophilus inluenza type b and meningococcus. Key measures to prevent
such infections include education, vaccination, prophylactic antimicrobial
therapy in selected patients, and early empirical therapy for febrile
epsisodes. It is critically important to educate patients regarding the
lifelong risk of postsplenectomy sepsis, the importance of vaccinations,
and the need for urgent action in response to a febrile episode.
Management of an Episode of Fever in an Asplenic Patient
Routine vaccines should be up to date including influenza, Tdap, Zoster,
HPV, MMR, Varicella. See CDSS Immunization section to order.
Ideally splenectomy vaccinations should be given 10 to 12 weeks before
elective splenectomy.  Where this is not possible they can be given up to
two weeks before or at least two weeks post-splenectomy.
Use of Antibiotic Prophylaxis for Asplenia:
Use of antibiotic prophylaxis, in addition to vaccination, further reduces
the risk of infection and poor outcomes.

From 10% to 40% of adults are colonized with Staphylococcus aureus, and the
anterior nares is the most common site of colonization. A majority of people
never have disease with S. aureus, but a tiny fraction of people develop
clinical infections with the S. aureus that has colonized their skin or anterior
nares. Steps to decolonize the skin and anterior nares can transiently diminish
or eradicate S. aureus colonization and can prevent post-operative wound
infection in certain high-risk circumstances. For people who have other forms of
recurrent S. aureus disease, not associated with an operation, results with
decolonization have been disappointing, and decolonization is not routinely
recommended. Colonization typically reappears in most patients within a few days
or weeks after decolonization has been attempted. Clinicians occasionally wish
to attempt decolonization for patients with frequent, troublesome recurrences.
The procedure here is one of several that have been studied, but none have been
particularly effective over the long run.
Consultation with Infectious Diseases is recommended.

Contents.Text: Stasis dermatitis is a common condition that is often confused with
bacterial cellulitis. Stasis dermatitis does not benefit from antimicrobial
therapy. It is important to distinguish between the two. The provider
should be mindful of the fact that bacterial cellulitis can occur on skin
with underlying stasis dermatitis. (See link below for bacterial cellulitis)
Common risk factors for venous stasis include advancing age, family
history of venous disease, increased body mass index, smoking, a history of
trauma, prior venous thrombosis and pregnancy. Chronic venous disease and
arterial vascular disease have some common risk factors (eg, smoking,
obesity) and pathophysiological processes. The most common symptoms reported
by patients with chronic venous disease are limb discomfort (tired, heavy
legs), pain, and limb swelling. Swelling is often worse with prolonged
standing and improves with leg elevation and walking. The skin of the
anterior surfaces of the lower legs often has brown or blue-grey
People with venous stasis are prone to develop stasis dermatitis which
is one of the most common and earliest dermatologic signs of chronic venous
insufficiency. Stasis dermatitis is an inflammatory process that presents as
an eczematous rash characterized by itching, erythema, scaling, weeping,
erosions, and crusting. Longstanding cases may develop lipodermatosclerosis
a fibrosing panniculitis of the subcutaneous tissue. Lipodermatosclerosis
typically starts with a firm area of induration at the medial ankle. As the
process progresses, the entire leg lower leg can become involved with
extension up to the mid leg in more advanced cases. The skin overlying the
panniculitis is typically heavily pigmented and bound down to the
subcutaneous tissues. Brawny edema above the fibrotic area and on the foot
below is seen in advanced cases. Leukocytosis and fever are common in people
Chronic venous disease is the most common cause of leg ulcers. They
are usually found low on the medial ankle over a perforating vein, or along
the course of the great or small saphenous veins. They occur more proximally
if precipitated by trauma. Venous ulcers are not found on the forefoot or
above the level of the knee. Venous ulcers can be multiple or single, and
can be exquisitely tender, shallow, exudative and have a granulation base.
The ulcer borders are usually irregular but not undermined. They can extend
circumferentially around the leg if left untreated.
Arterial ulcers are typically painful, and punched out or stellate. The
surrounding skin is red and taut. Some arterial ulcers are pale - others have
a black or yellow eschar. They are often associated with trauma and commonly
occur on the foot over pressure points. There may be other signs of arterial
insufficiency on the lower limb including thin atrophic or hairless skin,
poor pedal pulses, diminished capillary refill, or hypertrophic deformed
Patients with stasis or lipodermatosclerosis are prone to bouts of
bacterial cellulitis, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus or encapsulated
streptococci. Typically, stasis dermatitis develops slowly, over a week or
more. It is often bilateral. The onset of bacterial cellulitis is usually
abrupt, typically developing over 1 or 2 days. Bacterial cellulitis often
starts in one area and spreads to adjacent areas. Bacterial cellulitis is
unilateral. Both can present with fever and leukocytosis.
In a patient with stasis and cellulitis and the physician is uncertain
about whether bacterial cellulitis is present, the physician should consider
a trial of bed rest, leg elevation, and if there is fluid overload, diuresis
If the cellulitis improves in 24-48 hours, antibacterial therapy and the
attendant adverse reactions can be avoided. If it is clear that bacterial
cellulitis has occurred, antimicrobial therapy should be given.

Syphilis is a sexually transmitted disease caused by the spirochete Treponema
pallidum that can manifest as a variety of signs or symptoms. Primary syphilis
typically consists of painless ulcers or chancre at the site of infection with
regional adenopathy. Secondary syphilis often includes a skin rash (disseminated
and/or including the palms and soles), fever, malaise, mucocutaneous lesions and
lymphadenopathy. Tertiary syphilis includes those with cardiovascular or
Latent syphilis is a period of disease when a patient does not have symptoms but
is found to be infected through serologic testing. Early latent syphilis refers
to latent syphilis acquired within the preceding year and late latent syphilis
refers to all other cases of latent syphilis. Neurosyphilis can occur at any
stage of syphilis with early manifestations (e.g. meningitis, stroke, vision or
hearing loss) occurring within the first months to years of infection and late
manifestations (e.g. dementia, tabes dorsalis) occurring after 10-30 years.
A presumptive diagnosis is made through use of a nontreponemal or serologic
test (i.e. rapid plasma reagin [RPR]) and a treponemal test (i.e. fluorescent
treponemal antibody absorbed [FTA-ABS]). Direct methods through darkfield
microscopy and direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) must be used for definitive
diagnosis since T. pallidum cannot be cultured.
Persons with sexual contact with a person with primary, secondary or early
latent syphilis within the last 90 days should be presumptively treated even if

Uncomplicated cystitis is defined as symptomatic bladder inflammation caused by
bacterial infections in people with structurally and neurogenically normal
urinary tract. Symptoms usually include dysuria, lower abdominal pain, and
urgency. Most cases of uncomplicated cystitis occur in pre-menopausal, non-
pregnant, sexually active young women and is commonly associated with
Enterobacteriaceae (e.g.  E. coli and Klebsiella sp.) and occasionally S.
Cystitis is considered complicated when it occurs in  pregnant women, people
with abnormalities of the urinary tract, immunocompromised individuals and those
who have persistent, recurrent, or relapsed infections, or treatment failure.
Diagnosis and treatment of complicated cystitis is discussed elsewhere.
The presence of pyuria (>7 wbc/hpf) or positive leukocyte esterase, urine
nitrate, or urine bacteria is not a sufficient indication for antibiotic
treatment. Asymptomatic bacteriuria occurs in patients who have bacteria in the
urine with no symptoms of cystitis, and with few exceptions, should not be
treated. Diagnosis and treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria is further

URETHRITIS ASSOCIATED WITH SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED DISEASES
The main differential in a person who presents with dysuria is between cystitis
and urethritis. Bacterial urethritis is more likely in people with mild
dysuria, onset over a few days, or recent sexual contact.
The two most common sexually transmitted urethritis pathogens are Neisseria
gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. Nucleic acid amplification tests for
these pathogens are more sensitive than culture and should be used for patients
at risk for sexually transmitted urethritis.

Contents.Text: Cystitis refers to infection of the urinary bladder, but inflammation often
extends into the urethra. Typical symptoms and signs include dysuria, increased
urinary frequency, urgency, and/or suprapubic tenderness.
Most cases of uncomplicated cystitis occur in pre-menopausal, non-pregnant,
Most cases of complicated cystitis are associated with Escherichia coli, but
more resistant pathogens occur, including the Gram-positive pathogens
staphylococci and enterococci. Urine culture should be obtained before
Cystitis is considered complicated when one or more of the following is present
> Structural abnormalities (e.g. presence of obstruction, catheter or
> Metabolic abnormalities that reduce local host defenses (e.g. diabetes,
> Treatment failure or relapse or recurrence of infection
When a patient presents with symptoms of cystitis, urinalysis should be
performed to check for the presence of white blood cells. Increased numbers of
leukocytes (usually >25) in the presence of cystitis symptoms indicates
inflammation and thus cystitis. The bacterial etiology is so predictable that
urine culture is unnecessary and empirical treatment is indicated. The
clinical significance of pyuria in the absence of cystitis symptoms is unclear.
Antimicrobial therapy is not indicated for pyuria in the absence of symptoms.

Vaginitis usually presents with discharge, itching, irritation, odor, or pain.
Bacterial vaginosis is the most common form of vaginitis. Normal hydrogen
peroxide and lactic acid producing vaginal flora, including Lactobacillus
species, is reduced and high concentrations of anaerobic bacterial pathogens are
present. Pathogenic bacteria commonly include Gardnerella vaginalis, Mycoplasma
hominis, Nobiluncus, Prevotella and other Gram-negative anaerobes.
Vaginal pH should be measured, and the specimen should be examined under the
microscope for identification of clue cells (epithelial cell coated with
bacteria). In bacterial vaginosis the vaginal pH is high (> 4.5), the discharge
is homogenous and gray-white, and the specimen has a positive amine or whiff
test characterized by a fishy odor before or after addition of 10% KOH.
Bacterial vaginosis nucleic acid amplification tests are available for common
pathogens to aide in identification of pathogen(s).
Bacterial vaginosis may be transmitted sexually. Patients at risk of sexually
transmitted infections should be assessed for treatment.

Contents.Text: PREVENTION OF ANTIVIRAL INFECTIONS IN A PATIENT WITH MALIGNANCY
Viral infections reactivate in a small percentage of people with malignancy.
Most viral infections in patients with hematologic malignancies or solid
tumors result from reactivation of asymptomatic latent infections,
predominantly of herpes viruses, including herpes simplex virus (HSV),
varicella zoster virus (VZV) and cytomegalovirus (CMV). Exogenous
respiratory tract infections caused by influenza, parainfluenza
or respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are less common.
The main risk factor for clinically relevant reactivation is profound
disruption of cellular immune response, usually due to chemotherapy.
The duration and severity of neutropenia are of lesser importance.

Contents.Text: PREVENTION OF ANTIVIRAL INFECTIONS IN A PATIENT WITH MALIGNANCY
Solid tumors do not significantly compromise the cellular immune system.
Therefore, patients are at low risk for opportunistic viral infections.
Documented invasive viral infections are very rare. Coincidental
mucocutaneous infections by herpes simplex are easily treated and do not
result in life-threatening invasive infections. Reactivation of
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) or Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is rarely observed.
In patients with acute leukemia, treatment is highly aggressive and consists
of a combination of various cytotoxic agents administered in sequential
cycles as induction, consolidation and maintenance therapy. Persistent, i.e.
>10 days and profound neutropenia (<500 neutrophils) regularly occurs and
correlates with the risk of developing fever and infections. Almost all viral
infections during neutropenia constitute reactivations of herpes viruses.
None of the available studies demonstrated an effect of antiviral prophylaxis
on the initiation of antibiotic treatment, number of febrile days, duration
of antibiotic treatment, and onset of opportunistic infections. Therefore, no
recommendation for antiviral prophylaxis in patients with acute leukemia can
Patients undergoing leukemia induction therapy should receive prophylaxis.
Rituximab is a monoclonal anti-CD-20 antibody used for treatment of
lymphomas. It leads to a profound depletion of circulating B-cells. B-cells
recover usually within 3-6 months after treatment. Prolonged administration
of rituximab (e.g., maintenance treatment >12 months) may result in a
significant decrease of levels of immunoglobulin M. Parvovirus B19 and JC-
papovavirus infections have been reported with maintenance rituximab therapy,
but drugs that would prevent these infections are not available. There is no
substantial increase in risk of reactivation of herpes viruses (including
Recommend routine testing for Hepatitis B virus prior to initiating Rituximab
and other Anti-CD20 antibody therapy in patients.

Contents.Text: The likelihood of colonization of an intravenous catheter increases with time,
increasing noticeably after 3 days. Patients whose catheters become colonized
may or may not develop local or systemic signs or symptoms. All types of
catheters are associated with risk of local and catheter-associated bacteremia.
Since central catheters are usually used for more days than peripheral
catheters, central catheters have a greater risk of catheter-associated
When catheter-related bacteremia is suspected, draw blood cultures from both the
catheter and a peripheral vein. Growth rate between the two cultures may be used
to determine if the source of bacteremia is likely catheter-associated. If the
catheter obtained culture's time to positivity is 2 hours or more before the
peripheral vein obtained culture's time to positivity, this suggests catheter-
associated infection. Sample any exudate at the catheter site for gram stain and
Suppurative thrombophlebitis presents with inflammation in and around a vein.
There may be local thrombosis and/or bacteremia. Cases may be life-threatening
For patients with catheter-associated bacteremia with virulent pathogens like
Staphylococcus aureus, gram-negative bacilli, or candida, catheter removal is
almost always necessary. For mild or moderate cases with less virulent
organisms like coagulase-negative staphylococci, antimicrobial therapy is
successful without catheter removal about half of the time. The decision about
whether to remove the catheter depends on severity of illness, the need for the
catheter, and how difficult catheter replacement would be.
For cases in which an infected catheter is not removed, the success rate is
improved when the infected catheter is filled with an antimicrobial solution
during periods when the catheter is not used. Consult Infectious Diseases or

Surgical prophylaxis is indicated for open procedures and high-risk laparoscopic
procedures.  Additional doses should not be given after incisions are closed.
The risk of infectious complications after laparoscopic cholecystectomy is
increased after emergent procedures, procedures lasting more than 120 minutes,
intraoperative gall bladder rupture or bile spillage, conversion from
laparoscopic to open cholecystectomy, and insertion of a prosthetic device.
The risk is increased in patients who have had an episode of colic or a biliary
procedure within 30 days before the procedure, patients with acute cholecystitis
or jaundice, patients with a nonfunctional gallbladder, patients with
immunosuppression, pregnancy, diabetes, age greater than 70 years, or American
Society of Anesthesiologists classification of 3 or greater.
If one of these risk factors exists, prophylaxis is indicated for laparoscopic
cholecystectomy.  If there is a substantial likelihood that one of these risk
factors will develop during a procedure, the surgeon may elect to order

Contents.Text: Diagnosis of chronic sinusitis is based on presence of at least 2 of the 4
cardinal signs/symptoms lasting >/= 12 weeks. In addition, diagnosis requires
objective evidence of mucosal inflammation using nasal endoscopy and/or CT
imaging. The initial therapy for chronic sinusitis is treatment with intranasal
corticosteroids and saline. For patients with severe nasal blockage by polyps,
treat with a short course of oral glucocorticoids. Reassess patient after 1 to 3
months of intranasal therapy or after completion of glucocorticoid therapy. If
signs/symptoms have not improved, consult surgery, ENT and Infectious Diseases
Acute exacerbations of chronic sinusitis can be caused by discontinuing medical
therapy, viral infections, allergens, noxious inhalants and bacterial or fungal
infections. Bacterial infections should be suspected when the patient has
increased signs/symptoms persisting for more than 10 days. Refer to Severe
Sinusitis recommendations for choice of antimicrobial therapy in these patients.
Repeated use of the same agent should be avoided to prevent promotion of drug
resistant bacteria or increased fungal colonization.

Contents.Text: Patients with reduced CMI include those with HIV/AIDS, hematologic malignancies,
cytotoxic chemotherapy, and congenital abnormalities.  Patients with cell-
mediated immune defects are more susceptible to infections from ubiquitous
microorganisms that do not usually cause infection in healthy patients.  The
specific organisms that are more likely to be associated with disease vary
depending on the specific type of immune defect present, but include:
Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly Pneumocystis carinii), Mycobacterium avium,
Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Salmonella spp., Candida spp., Aspergillus spp.,
Toxoplasma gondii, varicella-zoster virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus,
These infectious diseases usually have a subacute or chronic presentation.  The
best approach in most circumstances is for the clinician to conduct a methodical
diagnostic workup to identify the specific pathogen and guide therapy.
Empirical antimicrobials are not indicated for patients with CMI defects who
present only with fever.  Contact Infectious Disease for more information.

Conjunctivitis is associated with viral or bacterial pathogens. Viral
conjunctivitis presents with watery discharge. Bacterial infections are more
likely to present with thick exudate and conjunctival injection. Allergic
conjunctivitis typically presents with stringy mucus. If there is pus
(hypopion), corneal involvement, possible bacterial conjunctivitis, or
Viral conjunctivitis is most commonly caused by adenovirus. It is self-limited
and antivirals provide no benefit. Symptomatic treatment with ophthalmic
antihistamine/decongestants and warm or cool compresses may relieve symptoms.
Bacterial conjunctivitis is most commonly associated with Staphylococcus aureus,
Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus spp., Moraxella catarrhalis,
Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Neisseria spp. or enteric gram-negative rods. It is
generally self-limited, but topical antimicrobials reduce duration of symptoms
and limit person-to-person spread of infection. If symptoms do not improve after

1 to 2 weeks followed by oral therapy.  For mild cases, start with oral therapy

Contents.Text: INTERIM RESULTS: GRAM-POSITIVE COCCI IN PAIRS
Aerobic Gram-positive cocci in pairs are usually streptococci, staphylococci, or
enterococci.These bacteria can be isolated under either aerobic or anaerobic
conditions.  Gram-positive cocci in pairs and clusters are usually
staphylococci.  Gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains are usually streptococci
or enterococci.  Gram-positive cocci in "chains" are likely streptococci.  If
the lab reports Gram-positive cocci in "short chains", enterococci are likely.

on the scalp.  Dead nits may remain for months after successful treatment.  Dead
nits are usually located more than 6 mm from the scalp.
Lice are often transmitted by infected clothing and bedclothes but not by

Contents.Text: Humans are protected by a broad array of host defenses that fall into two major
categories: innate and immune host defenses.  Innate defense operate
continuously without specific antigenic stimulation and immune defenses are
primed by and respond to antigenic stimulation.
Each type of host defense protects against a specific set of organisms.  As a
result, infectious diseases more common because of host defense defects in an
individual patient are usually predictable from that patient's host defense
defects.  For example, antibody or complement deficiencies predispose patients
to disease with encapsulated organisms but not fungi.  Defects in cell-mediated
immunity predispose patients to infections with mycobacteria or cytomegalovirus
but not Escherichia coli or influenza virus.  Suspected cases of infectious
disease must be evaluated in the context of the patient's host defects.
Management, including possible antimicrobial therapy, should be initiated on the
basis of the most likely offending pathogens.

Contents.Text: Several types of neurological dysfunction predispose patients to infectious
diseases.  Comatose patients are unable to keep weight off dependent tissues,
predisposing them to decubitus ulcers and pressure necrosis.  Atelectasis is
common in obtunded patients who cannot cough or breathe deeply.  When patients
require artificial ventilation, intubation compounds the risk of respiratory
Neurological dysfunction of the bladder can interfere with normal bladder
emptying and predisposes patients to bacteriuria.  The risk of bacteruria
increases if patients are catheterized.  Antimicrobial treatment is not
indicated for asymptomatic bacteriuria.  It provides no benefit and increases
risk of colonization with resistant organisms.
Neurological dysfunction predisposes patients to aspiration of oropharyngeal or
gastric contents.  Aspiration causes fever, inflammation, and/or pulmonary
infiltrate, but does not require antimicrobial treatment. Bacterial pneumonia
occurs in a minority of patients who experience significant aspiration,
typically about 3 days later.  Typically, the patient improves for the first 2
days and then worsens as bacterial pneumonia develops with increased fever, new
or progressive infiltrates, leukocytosis, and newly purulent sputum.

have also been associated with corneal infection. Obtain corneal scrapings for

based on Ophthalmology and/or Infectious Diseases recommendations. Ophthalmic
corticosteroids are contraindicated in patients with keratitis.

Contents.Text: Patients who have been bitten while in endemic areas of New England, Mid-
Atlantic States, Minnesota, and Wisconsin where local rate of Ixodes spp. tick
infection rate with Borrelia burgdorferi in an endemic area may be treated with
prophylactic antibiotics for prevention of Lyme disease. Using a wait and see
method by monitoring for signs and symptoms of Lyme disease is also an
acceptable approach in patients who have been bitten by an Ixodes spp. tick.
All following criteria must be met to be considered for prophylactic treatment
1. Doxycycline is not contraindicated (i.e. allergy, pregnant, lactating)
2. Attached tick is reliably identified as an adult or nymphal Ixodes spp.
Follow link below for identification guide:
3. Tick is attached for greater than or equal to 36 hours based on degree of
tick engorgement with blood or likely time of exposure to tick infested area.
4. Prophylaxis must be started within 72 hours after time tick was removed.
5. Patient was exposed to tick bite in endemic areas where rate of Ixodes
scapularis infection with Borrelia burgdorferi is greater than 20%. Minnesota
counties where there is high risk of tickborne disease are shown in the
Providers can call the Minnesota Department of Health (651-201-5414) or the
Wisconsin Department of Health Services (608-266-1865) for specific rates of B.
burdorferi infection of Ixodes spp. ticks in area where a patient was exposed.

ERYTHEMA MIGRANS ASSOCIATED WITH LYME DISEASE
For pregnant patients or those with contraindications to doxycycline:
Erythema migrans is the first manifestation of Lyme disease in 70-80% of cases.
It is typically an erythematous circular rash, 5cm or larger in diameter, with
induration and central clearing (although other patterns occur). It usually
develops at the site of the bite and/or in one or more distant locations. The
rash occurs 3 to 30 days after the bite. Rashes with onset less than 3 days
after a tick bite are not from Lyme disease.

Acute mastoiditis most commonly occurs as a suppurative complication of acute
otitis media. Diagnosis is supported by CT or MRI imaging and culture of
drainage. Antibiotics and drainage of middle ear are sufficient treatment in
most cases. Mastoidectomy is necessary if abscess has formed in the mastoid
bone. If complication of first episode of acute otitis media, etiologies
typically include Streptococcus pneumonia (most common), Streptococcus pyogenes,
or Staphylococcus aureus. If secondary to chronic otitis media, etiologies
typically include Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Patients
usually too ill for outpatient therapy. ENT consultation recommended. Obtain
cultures of auditory canal or middle ear fluid (preferred).
<AND> vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q 12 hours ($) [R] for 7 days
Step down treatment after initial intravenous antibiotic treatment in patients
who can tolerate oral therapy. Base selection on culture results. Adjust for a
total duration of 7 days of antimicrobial therapy.
Chronic mastoiditis is usually the result of chronic otitis media with
perforation of the tympanic membrane. There is often associated formation of a
cholesteatoma (keratoma). Diagnosis is supported by CT or MRI imaging and
culture of drainage. Long term treatment with topical antimicrobials is first
line therapy. Infection is often polymicrobial, including Staphylococcus aureus,
Pseudomonas aeruginosa and anaerobes. Treatment should be managed in
collaboration with otolaryngology and includes topical antimicrobials, care of
external auditory canal, and is some cases mastoidectomy. If possible, withhold
therapy until a pathogen is identified by culture of drainage to direct therapy.
Specific drug choice dictated by culture results.

Community-acquired bacterial sinusitis is most often due to Streptococcus
pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae or Moraxella catarrhalis. Streptococci,
Staphylococcus aureus and anaerobes are isolated less frequently.
Treatment for first 10 days of illness
Treat with decongestants, analgesics, and nasal saline spray.
Treatment of cases that have not improved in 10 days despite
treatment with decongestants, analgesics, and nasal saline.
If symptoms worsen despite 72 hours or  fail to improve after 3-5 days of
initial empirical antimicrobial therapy, broaden coverage, switch to different
antimicrobial class and treat 7-10 days. If symptoms continue to worsen or there
is no improvement after 3-5 more days of treatment, obtain CT to investigate
non-infectious or suppurative causes. ENT consultation is recommended. If
sinuses are aspirated, specimens should be cultured.

MORE ABOUT PHARYNGITIS/ TONSILLITIS AND THE MODIFIED CENTOR SCORE
As most cases are of viral origin, antimicrobials are not indicated in these
cases. Warm saltwater gargle rinses and throat lozenges provide temporary relief
of throat pain. Five to 10% of cases are caused by group A Streptococcus.
Antimicrobial treatment reduces symptoms by one day, prevents suppurative
complications and prevents acute rheumatic fever, an uncommon disease in US
Streptococcal pharyngitis or tonsillitis should be suspected when patients have
fever and exudate on the pharyngeal wall or tonsils without symptoms like cough,
nasal congestion, or runny nose that suggest viral infection or common cold. If
streptococcal pharyngitis is suspected in adults, perform PCR testing for group
A streptococci and treat only if positive.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a rare cause of pharyngitis. N. gonorrhoeae should be
considered for patients with risk factors for sexually transmitted diseases. N.
gonorrhoeae infections must be reported to the state health department and this
will be done by Infection Control if the culture is positive.

Contents.Text: Call Surgery immediately and consult Infectious Diseases in all cases.
Necrotizing infections involve tissues skin and/or deeper structures, including
fascia and muscle.  These infections destroy tissue, often rapidly, and are
often fatal if not treated promptly and appropriately.  Necrotizing infections
usually result from trauma, surgery, and/or ischemia.  These infections can be
monomicrobial (e.g., with streptococci or clostridia) or polymicrobial (usually
with a mixture of aerobes and anaerobes).  Fournier gangrene is usually
associated with mixed infection.  Myonecrosis is most commonly associated with
Necrotizing infections differ from cellulitis in several ways.  Necrotic
infections typically have one or more of the following: (1) severe, constant
pain, (2) bullae, (3) bruising or necrosis of overlying skin, (4) gas in tissues
which can be felt or seen on images, (5) edema that extends beyond areas of
erythema, (6) local anesthesia, and (7) signs of systemic toxicity, such as
fever, leukocytosis, delirium, or renal failure.
Necrotizing infections must be treated with both antimicrobial therapy and
surgical procedures (excision and/or drainage).  Call surgery to see the patient
immediately in all cases.  Obtain tissue and blood cultures and begin empirical
antimicrobials.  For several necrotic diseases and/or pathogens, a combination
of two antimicrobials is recommended including a bactericidal antimicrobial
active at the cell wall or membrane (e.g., beta-lactam or glycopeptide) and an
antimicrobial that rapidly inhibits protein synthesis and thus inhibits toxin
Repeat debridement should be performed daily until no further debridement is
necessary. Antibiotic therapy should be tailored as soon as culture results
Administer antibiotics until further debridement is no longer necessary, the
patient has improved clinically, and fever has been absent for 48-72 hours.
