Contents.Text: Bacteremia occurs several times a day during the course of daily activities
like eating and brushing teeth and rarely results in endocarditis, even in
people with abnormal valves.  While bacteremia might occur following dental
or other procedures, most cases of endocarditis are from the millions more
episodes of transient bacteremia a person experiences per year from ordinary
daily activities.  There is no evidence that antimicrobial prophylaxis
prevents endocarditis after procedures.  The best available evidence suggests
that prophylactic antimicrobials confer more risks than benefits in most
situations.  A decision about whether to administer antimicrobial prophylaxis
should be based on both the risk of endocarditis conferred by the patient's
cardiac defect and the risk of bacteremia from a planned dental or surgical
For complete information follow this link:
Determine the need for prophylaxis through the 2-step process outlined
Step 1.  Assess the risk of endocarditis for your patient
Prophylaxis is recommended if a patient has any of the following conditions:
>>  Certain specific congenital heart conditions - refer to the full guidelines
(link above) or consult Cardiology for more detailed recommendations
>>  Cardiac transplant that develops a problem in the heart valve
Note: Prophylaxis is NO LONGER RECOMMENDED for patients with:
>>  Congenital heart conditions such as ventricular septal defect, atrial
Step 2.  Assess the risk of bacteremia from the planned procedure
Prophylaxis is indicated for these procedures:
>>  All dental procedures that involve manipulation of gingival tissue or the
periapical region of teeth or perforation of the oral mucosa. (see notes)
>>  Procedures on the respiratory tract that involve incision or biopsy of
the respiratory mucosa, such as tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy.
Prophylaxis is recommended for bronchoscopy when procedure involves
incision of the respiratory tract mucosa.
>>  Procedures that involve incision through infected skin, skin structures,
>>  Dermatologic procedures that breach the oral mucosa.
Notes: Prophylaxis is NO LONGER RECOMMENDED for these procedures:
routine anesthetic injections through noninfected tissue, taking
dental radiographs, placement of removable prosthodontic or
orthodontic appliances, adjustment of orthodontic appliances,
placement of orthodontic brackets, shedding of deciduous teeth, and
bleeding from trauma to the lips or oral mucosa.
Wilson et al.  Prevention of Infective Endocarditis:Circulation 2007

Lice are parasitic insects. Human lice survive by feeding on human blood.

The presence of nits on a hair shaft, especially when they are located more
than 6 mm from the skin, does NOT indicate active infestation. Nits may remain
present for months after successful treatment.
Household contacts and persons who may have come into contact with personal
belongings of an infested individual should be examined for evidence of lice
and discarded or cleaned if contaminated.

Contents.Text: Per the Sepsis-3 task force, sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ
dysfunction caused by dysregulated host response to infection.
Septic shock is a subset of sepsis in which profound circulatory, cellular, and
metabolic abnormalities occur. Septic shock requires vasopressor therapy and is
associated with in-hospital mortality greater than 40%.
Early intervention is crucial to prevention of death from sepsis. Antimicrobials
active against likely pathogens, based on source infection, and supportive
treatment to maintain vascular perfusion should be initiated immediately (within
the first hour of patient presentation). Reassess antimicrobial therapy daily to
narrow therapeutic spectrum when culture and susceptibility data are available.

blistering and exfoliation resulting from toxins produced by Staphylococcus
aureus.  SSSS is usually found in children and rarely in older adults.  Obtain
a skin biopsy to differentiate between SSSS and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Initiate anti-staphylococcal therapy and obtain cultures and susceptibilities.

If cultures reveal methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), change
to nafcillin or cefazolin for better antimicrobial activity.

Contents.Text: CRITERIA FOR DIAGNOSIS OF STREPTOCOCCAL TOXIC SHOCK SYNDROME
These criteria were developed for epidemiological purposes.  Treat cases when
fewer criteria are met if streptococcal TSS seems likely.
1.)  Isolation of Group A Streptococcus from a normally sterile site (eg, blood
cerebrospinal, pleural, or peritoneal fluid, tissue biopsy, or surgical wound)
2.)  Hypotension (systolic blood pressure 90 mm Hg in adults
3.)  Two or more of the following:
(creatinine in adults, 2 mg/dL, in children, two-times upper limit of normal
for age, in patients with pre-existing renal disease two-fold elevation over
(eg, two-times upper limit of normal for age of transaminases or bilirubin, in
patients with pre-existing liver disease two-fold elevation over baseline)
Soft tissue necrosis (eg, necrotizing fasciitis, myositis, or gangrene)

Contents.Text: PATIENTS WITH SIGNS OF INFECTION MORE THAN 48 HOURS AFTER PROCEDURE
Most post-operative infections appear at least 4 days after the operation.  If
the wound appears normal to examination surgical site infection is unlikely.
Seek other source of fever.  Consider opening wounds that show induration or
erythema.  Obtain material for gram stain and culture whenever possible.
Determine whether the patient has signs of invasive or systemic infection like
erythema (diameter greater than 5 centimeters), temperature greater than 38.5
degrees Celsius (101.3 degrees Fahrenheit) or heart rate higher than 100 beats
If there are no signs of invasive or systemic infection systemic antimicrobials
are unnecessary.  Dressing changes alone are indicated.
For wounds that require complicated care
If there are signs of invasive or systemic infection obtain blood cultures and
wound Gram stain and cultures.  Whenever possible select antimicrobial therapy
based on the Gram stain.  When the Gram stain cannot provide guidance give
Empirical treatment of INFECTED WOUNDS AFTER CLEAN SURGERY or wounds on the
trunk, head, neck, arms or legs
Vancomycin should be included in the initial regimen due to the prevalence of
methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.  However beta-lactam antibiotics
are more effective for susceptible bacteria than is vancomycin.  If methicillin-

Surgical site infections are categorized by the extent of tissues involved.
Superficial incisional infections involve only the subcutaneous space and occur
within 30 days of operation.  Deep incisional infections involve deep layers of
soft tissue, such as fascia and muscle, and occur within 30 days of operation,
or within 1 year of operation if prosthetic material was inserted.  Organ/space
infections involve anatomical areas other than the incisional wound that were
opened or manipulated during operation.  Organ/space infections should be
treated as infections of the relevant area of the anatomy.  Return to the main
page and choose the pertinent organ system for advice on management of these
Post-operative wound infections usually occur between 2 and 30 days after the
operation.  Infections within 48 hours of the surgery are uncommon, but are
serious when they do occur.  Symptoms commonly begin to appear no sooner than 5
days after the operation and may take up to 2 weeks to appear.

Potential pathogens are introduced into normally sterile areas of the body
during most surgical procedures.  The purpose of antimicrobial prophylaxis is to
reduce the intraoperative microbial burden so that local host defenses can
eliminate microorganisms and prevent disease.  Prophylaxis cannot be expected to
Antimicrobial agent for surgical prophylaxis should be:
1) active against the pathogens most likely to contaminate the surgical site
2) given in an appropriate dosage and at a time that ensures adequate serum and
tissue concentrations during the period of potential contamination
4) administered for the shortest effective period to minimize adverse effects,
the development of resistance, and costs.
Most experts do not recommend routine use of broad-spectrum antibiotics such as
ertapenem or extended spectrum cephalosporins such as cefotaxime, ceftriaxone,
ceftazidime, cefepime or ceftaroline for surgical prophylaxis because they are
expensive, some less active against staphylococci than first or second
generation cephalosporins, and their spectrum of activity often includes
organisms rarely encountered in elective surgery.

Although many patients have drug allergies documented in their medical records,
the symptoms or circumstances associated with the allergies are rarely
documented. Several studies have demonstrated that the incidence of true drug
"allergy" is lower than that suggested by what is recorded in medical records.
Because beta-lactam antimicrobials often represent agents of choice for
prophylaxis, the medical history should be adequate to determine if the patient
likely had a true allergy (e.g., anaphylaxis, urticaria, angioedema,
bronchospasm, hypotension, or arrhythmia) or a serious adverse drug
reaction(e.g., drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome, drug fever, or toxic
The incidence of adverse effects to cephalosporins among patients with reported
penicillin allergy is rare (3-5%).  However cephalosporins should be avoided in
patients who report serious allergic reactions to penicillin like anaphylaxis,
urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, or arrhythmia.

Contents.Text: PATIENTS WITH SIGNS OF INFECTION WITHIN 48 HOURS OF PROCEDURE
Fever within 48 hours of procedure is usually due to anesthesia or other non-
infectious factors but Clostridium species and Streptococcus pyogenes can cause
early infections.  Examine the wound of any patient with systemic signs of
infection, like fever, within 48 hours of surgery.  If there are signs of
infection consider opening the wound.  Obtain a STAT Gram stain and culture of
any drainage. If the Gram stain shows evidence of streptococci or clostridia
refer to the section on necrotizing infections.  If signs of wound infection are
absent seek an alternative source of the fever.

SURGICAL WOUND CLASSIFICATION AND ANTIMICROBIAL PROPHYLAXIS RECOMMENDATIONS
A wound resulting from a procedure in which no inflammation or infection was
encountered and the respiratory, alimentary, genital, or uninfected urinary
tract was not entered.  Clean wounds are closed at the end of surgery and if
drainage is necessary wounds are closed with drains in place.
Antimicrobial prophylaxis is usually not indicated.  Exceptions are procedures
in which prosthetic material will be inserted or for operations in which a
surgical site infection would be catastrophic.  These exceptions include most
cardiac operations, joint replacement, revascularization procedures in legs, and
Clean-contaminated wounds are those in which the respiratory, alimentary,
genital, or urinary tracts are entered but there is no evidence of infection and
there is no major break in technique.  These include operations on the biliary
Antimicrobial prophylaxis is indicated for most of these procedures.
Contaminated wounds include an open, fresh, accidental wound, or operations with
major breaks in sterile technique, gross spillage from the gastrointestinal
tract, or incisions in which acute, non-purulent inflammation is encountered.
Antimicrobials are therapeutic and not prophylactic.
Dirty-infected wounds are old traumatic wounds with devitalized tissue and those
that involve existing infection or perforated viscera.  The organisms usually
have been present in the operative field since before the operation.
Antimicrobials are therapeutic and not prophylactic.

Contents.Text: Organ transplantation is associated with many host defense defects.  Early on,
surgical wounds may become infected.  Preparation for transplantation and anti-
rejection drugs can induce neutropenia.  Later, CMI defects predominate.
Patients become infected with exogenous pathogens and also endogenous pathogens
like cytomegalovirus that might have been present in latent or subclinical form.
Cell-mediated immune defects caused by anti-rejection drugs cause patients to be
especially susceptible to infections with organisms that infrequently cause
disease in healthy people.  They include: Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly
Pneumocystis carinii), mycobacteria, salmonella, candida, aspergillus,
Toxoplasma gondii, varicella-zoster virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus,
The approach to fever or other signs or symptoms suggesting the possibility of
an infectious disease depends on the specific defects present in the patient,
the nature of the presenting signs and symptoms and a bedside assessment of the
severity of illness.  Empirical antimicrobials are usually not indicated for
fever alone unless the patient has a host defense defect that predisposes to
rapid progression of illness like severe neutropenia or splenectomy.  Contact
Rich RR, et al, eds.  Clinical Immunology
Roitt I, et al, eds.  Immunology

Patients with signs and symptoms of sepsis, like multiple organ system
dysfunction, shock and/or acute renal failure, should be treated as outlined in
the sepsis pathway. Early intervention is crucial to prevention of death from
sepsis. Sepsis is discussed in more detail in the systemic infections section.
Obtain blood cultures before starting antibiotics when signs or symptoms suggest
bacteremia. Obtain 2 blood culture sets from different venipuncture sites 15
minutes apart. When suspicion is strong and the patient's signs and symptoms
have not responded, obtain 2 blood culture sets 15 minutes apart the next day.
Bacteremia is discussed in more detail in the systemic infections section.
When patients who require paraenteral therapy are afebrile, clinically stable,
and can take oral medication, convert to oral therapy based on the
identification and susceptibility of the isolate.
Antimicrobial treatment duration is based on pathogen isolated from blood
cultures and patient response to therapy, typically 7-14 days.

Contents.Text: The decision to treat should be based on clinical symptoms and/or presence of
a high risk condition, and should NOT be delayed until laboratory test
It is important to use antiviral drugs early to treat influenza in people who
are very sick with influenza (for example hospitalized people) and people who
are sick with influenza and have a greater chance of getting severe
complications. If a patient is not in a high-risk group or is not hospitalized,
healthcare providers should use clinical judgment to guide treatment decisions.
People who have a greater chance of serious influenza complications include:
*Pregnant women and women up to 2 weeks from end of pregnancy
*People with certain chronic medical conditions (such as asthma, heart
failure, chronic lung disease) and people with a weak immune system (due to
illnesses such as diabetes and HIV)
*People younger than 19 years of age who are receiving long-term aspirin
If indicated, antivirals should be started as soon as possible.  Maximal
benefit occurs when started within 48 hours of symptom onset.  However,
antivirals should not be withheld if symptoms began more than 48 hours prior
and the patient meets criteria for treatment and remains severely ill.
Oseltamivir or zanamivir are the only two antiviral drugs the Center for
Disease Control is recommending for this flu season. Neither amantadine nor
rimantadine are recommended for treatment or chemoprophylaxis this flu season.
Duration of antiviral treatment is 5 days.  Extending the treatment may be
needed for those patients with prolonged illness or who are immnunosuppresed.

Contents.Text: The preferred route of antimicrobial therapy is by mouth.  Intravenous
metronidazole should only be used when oral therapy cannot be used to deliver
drug to the colon.  Intravenous vancomycin does not get into colonic contents
ANTIBIOTIC ASSOCIATED COLITIS (CLOSTRIDIUM DIFFICILE COLITIS) WITHOUT ILEUS OR
Discontinue implicated antibiotic and avoid high risk antibiotic if antibiotic
Medium:  penicillins and narrow-spectrum cephalosporins, carbapenems,
No risk: sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, methenamine, fosfomycin
Avoid antiperistaltic agents (narcotics, loperamide, etc).  There is increased
evidence that antacid therapy, especially with proton pump inhibitors
and histamine receptor blockers, increases the risk for C. difficile disease
and the risk of recurrences.  Avoid antacid therapy in patients without clear
indications, especially for those at risk for C. difficile disease or who
have had an episode and are at risk for recurrence.
Most cases respond to antimicrobial therapy for C. difficile colitis,
especially if other antimicrobial therapy has been stopped.  Relapse is
usually due to failure of normal colonic flora to re-establish itself, rather
than antimicrobial treatment failure.  If symptoms do not respond to
antimicrobials, re-consider diagnosis.  Relapse occurs in 6% to 25% of people
after their first episode of C. difficile associated disease.

Contents.Text: COLONIZED RESPIRATORY TRACT IN A PATIENT ON A VENTILATOR
The respiratory tracts of persons who are intubated, have a
tracheostomy, or have other abnormalities of the larynx or trachea are
usually colonized with bacteria and often fungi. The bacteria can be of
relatively low virulence (e.g. coagulase negative staphylococci, streptococci,
candida) or of potentially greater virulence (Staphylococcus aureus,
enterobacteriaceae, pseudomonas). Candida and enterococci are common
respiratory tract colonizers and they almost never cause pneumonia. There is
no benefit from treatment of patients with systemic antimicrobials simply
because the respiratory tract is colonized with a potential pathogen and there
is no evidence of an infiltrate. Systemic antimicrobial therapy will select for
resistant organisms and may lead to other adverse effects.
Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for ventilator-associated pneumonia
treatment recommendations in patients with a new or progressive infiltrate and
at least one of the following: fever greater than 100.4F, leukocytosis,
Kalil et al. Clin Infect Dis, 2016, 63(5): e61-e111.

Contents.Text: Open wounds are usually colonized with bacteria and often fungi. This is true of
ulcers (see below), post-operative wounds, traumatic wounds, and others. Then
bacteria can be of relatively low virulence (eg, coagulase negative
staphylococci, diphtheroids) or of potentially greater virulence (Staphylococcus
aureus, enterobacteriaceae, pseudomonas). Candida is commonly present on wounds
that are moist or covered. There is no need to treat patients with systemic
antimicrobials simply because a wound culture is positive for a potential
pathogen. Topical antimicrobials are not effective in nearly all circumstances
and can select for resistant organisms or lead to other adverse effects.
Systemic antimicrobial therapy may be indicated if there are signs of infection.

Antibiotics are used to prevent infections in patients undergoing surgery in
certain well-defined circumstances. They are used to prevent surgical site
infection or to prevent endocarditis in circumstances where the risk of
endocarditis is high. For many low-risk surgeries, the risks associated with
antibiotic use, which can be severe or cause death, outweigh the benefits. The
following recommendations are consistent with guidelines published by the
American Heart Association and Infectious Disease Society of America.
In general, antibiotics are used to prevent post-operative wound infection
in clean-contaminated surgery. Most dermatological surgery involves clean
sites, and the risks of antibiotics outweigh potential benefits. Antibiotics
are used to prevent endocarditis and hematogenous joint infection in procedures
involving the oral mucosa or infected skin. Antibitic prophylaxis is also
recommended to prevent surgical site infections in procedures involving high
When they are used, prophylactic oral antimicrobial agents should be
administered 30-60 minutes before the first tissue manipulation or incision.
Intravenous antimicrobials should be administered 60 minutes (120 minutes for
Antimicrobials should not be used to prevent infections in patients with
vascular grafts or orthopedic prostheses because the risk of bacteremia or
infection of these devices is tiny and antibiotic risks outweigh any theoretical
A full course of antibiotics should be used to treat skin infections where
infection is already present at the time of surgery.
Suggested antibiotic prophylaxis regimens should be targeted against the typical
pathogens likely to be present. A risk-based approach for coverage of MRSA
should be taken in patients with specific risk factors for MRSA.

Contents.Text: Early treatment as alternative to chemoprophylaxis:
In most cases, if a person is suspected of having been exposed to influenza,
early treatment should signs or symptoms develop is preferred rather than
The provider should explain the early signs and symptoms of influenza to the
patient and advise the patient to immediately contact a health care provider
for evaluation and possible early treatment if these symptoms or signs
develop. Influenza-like symptoms or signs include fever, cough, sore throat,
runny or stuffy nose, body aches, headache, chills, fatigue, vomiting, and
diarrhea. Influenza can present without fever.
Health care providers should use clinical judgment regarding situations where
early recognition of illness and treatment might be an appropriate
Early treatment alternative or chemoprophylaxis may be considered for:
*Persons who are part of a high-risk group and are household or close
contacts of someone with influenza-like illness
*Health care personnel who have occupational exposures
*Resident of a long term care facility that had close contact with another
resident or staff with influenza-like illness.
*Atypical situations (such as case clusters). ContactDepartment of Health
Duration of antiviral treatment is 10 days.  Among long-term care residents,
the antiviral use should be re-evaluated after 10 days. If no further
exposures have occurred, antivirals should be discontinued.

Patients who appear to be developing fulminant hepatitis, including those with

is suggested by increased prothrombin time, cholestasis, ascites, decreased
liver size, or decreasing serum albumin. Supportive treatment includes
maintenance of fluid and electrolyte balance, monitoring and possible correction
of coagulation defects, treatment of hepatic encephalopathy, and good nutrition
Prevention for persons with continuing high risk of disease
Vaccine should be offered to persons at high risk of hepatitis A infection: men
who have sex with men, travelers to endemic areas likely to be exposed, illegal
drug users, persons at occupational risk of disease, persons with chronic liver
Give Hepatitis A vaccine 1 ml IM x 2, separated by 6 to 12 months
Prevention for persons with a specific, defined exposure
Post-exposure prophylaxis should be offered to persons with substantial exposure
to hepatitis A. Specifically, persons exposed to acute hepatitis through
household or sexual contact, persons who attend or work in a day care center
with a recent case, or employee or patron of a restaurant with a food handler
with hepatitis. Post exposure prophylaxis must be given within 2 weeks of
exposure. Vaccine can be given at the same time as immune-globulin.

Contents.Text: Ocular herpes infection can be caused by either HSV-1 or HSV-2. The majority of
cases are caused by HSV-1. The recurrence rate of ocular herpes is 40% over a 5
year period, less than that of oral or genital herpes. Ocular herpes is a
major cause of blindness and typically presents as infection of the epithelium
of the cornea but can also rarely involve the stroma and endothelium.
Involvement of the stroma or endothelium requires treatment with topical
steroid and close monitoring. For these cases, start oral antiviral and consult
Antiviral prophylaxis is recommended for patients with multiple recurrences,
recurrent episodes with ulceration, recurrent inflammation with
scar/vascularization approaching visual axis, patients who have had keratoplasty
for HSV-related scarring/astigmatism, and patients who have had HSV keratitis
while on immunosuppressive therapy. Post-surgical prophylaxis is not discussed
here. Please consult ophthalmology for more information.

Contents.Text: HSV infection of the esophagus usually occurs in patients who are
immunocompromised, typically solid organ and bone marrow transplant
recipients. In healthy patients HSV esophagitis occurs occasionally,
usually in men under the age of 40.
Patients usually present with odynophagia and dysphagia. Fever
epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and heartburn are less frequent.
Some patients may have coexistent herpes labialis or oropharyngeal
ulcers. Diagnosis is usually established with an upper endoscopy.
Suggestive findings may also be seen during a barium swallow.
Spontaneous resolution usually occurs in immunocompetent patients after
one to two weeks. Patients may respond more quickly if treated with a
Treatment of mild to moderate disease

Contents.Text: Treatment of Candida Urinary Tract Infections
Asymptomatic bacteriuria (>= 100,000 bacteria per ml of urine) is common in
middle aged and older people, especially those who have chronic medical
conditions. Pyuria is common in persons with bacteriuria and individuals with
indwelling catheters in place. By itself, the presence of pyuria is not
sufficient to diagnose bacteriuria, and the presence or absence of pyuria does
not differentiate symptomatic from asymptomatic urinary infection. Candiduria is
less common than bacteriuria, but the implications of candiduria are similar to
Many studies, including randomized clinical trials have shown that
treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria and candiduria, with or without pyuria is
of no benefit, except in certain well-defined circumstances. Antimicrobial
therapy is always accompanied by risk of harms, including drug reactions,
Clostridium difficile colitis, anaphylaxis and death. Except in circumstances
specified below, it is best to not order urinalysis or urine culture in
asymptomatic persons. If bacteriuria, candiduria or pyuria is discovered in an
asymptomatic person for some reason, antimicrobial therapy should not be given
Pregnant women or patients undergoing urological procedures with bacteriuria

CONDITIONS NOT BENEFITTED BY ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY
Several common conditions associated with inflammation or
microorganisms do not benefit from antibiotic therapy in most or all cases.
Yet, antimicrobials are frequently prescribed for these conditions leading to
unnecessary toxicity and costs, rare deaths, and the relentless increase in
antimicrobial resistance. Please review these conditions and do not give
antimicrobials for these conditions unless there are extraordinary
circumstances that make your situation different. If you have any questions,
please contact the infectious disease physician on call.

Contents.Text: Infection of salivary tissue is a relatively common disease. It is usually
caused by a stone in the parotid duct, dehydration, or a viral infection.
Sialolithiasis in elderly patients often leads to ductal obstruction and
secondary infection. Other predisposing factors for ductal occlusion include
dehydration, anticholinergic medications such as tricyclics and diphenhydramine,
general disability and trauma. Once culture results are available adjust
antimicrobial therapy based on specific etiologic organism.

and analgesics and maintain good hydration to prevent secondary bacterial
infection. Other viral causes of parotitis include influenza and enteroviruses.

Suppurative Parotitis. Acute bacterial parotitis affects primarily elderly,
malnourished, dehydrated or post-operative patients. Symptoms include fever,
toxicity, and tender swelling along the mandible with purulent drainage from the
parotid duct. Suppurative parotitis is usually unilateral whereas viral
parotitis is usually bilateral. Pain is intense and aggressive, analgesic
therapy is required. Progression of infection may lead to massive swelling of
the neck, respiratory obstruction, septicemia and osteomyelitis of adjacent
facial bones. Empiric antibiotics are required for coverage of Staphylococcus
aureus if bacterial, and surgical drainage is usually necessary.
Chronic Parotitis. Parotitis is recurrent with intermittent acute exacerbations.
Chronic, low-grade bacterial infection results in functional destruction of the
salivary gland. It may be confused with Sjogren's syndrome, a noninfectious
illness. Therapy includes systemic antibiotics. Parotidectomy may eventually be
required for patients with long-standing infection.
Viral Parotitis. Mumps parotitis is characterized by the rapid, painful swelling
of one or both parotid glands within 2 to 3 weeks after exposure to the mumps
virus. Mumps usually involves both parotid glands whereas bacterial parotitis is
unilateral. Other viral causes of parotitis include influenza and enteroviruses.
Mumps parotitis usually resolves spontaneously in 5 to 10 days. Provide
symptomatic relief of pain and fever and maintain hydration to prevent secondary

Contents.Text: BLOOD CULTURE POSITIVE FOR COAGULASE NEGATIVE STAPHYLOCOCCI (CNS)
CNS are the most common contaminants isolated from blood cultures. When CNS
isolated from blood cultures represent true bacteremia, the blood is usually
obtained from a patient with plastic or metal in the body. The most common
source of coagulase negative staphylococcal bacteremia is an infected
When CNS are isolated from blood, the physician should carefully assess the
patient to decide whether the isolation represents disease or colonization.
Colonization is more likely if a single bottle is positive or both bottles from
a single blood draw are positive. If multiple bottles are positive from separate
blood draws, it is more likely that the isolates reflect disease or colonization
of an intravascular device. Isolates from contaminated bottles often take
several days to become positive. If the patient has risk factors for true
coagulase negative staphylococcal bacteremia, catheter-related blood stream
infection and/or the patient is severely ill, antimicrobials should be given. If
there is a plastic or metal prosthesis in the body, the physician should
evaluate the site for possible infection. If the isolates are likely to
represent contamination and the patient does not seem ill with CNS,
antimicrobial therapy would not be helpful and should not be given.

Contents.Text: Patients are given post-exposure prophylaxis based upon their risk including:
type of exposure, epidemiology of rabies in the area where contact occurred,
circumstances of the exposure incident, species and the availability of animal
involved. The Nebraska Department of Health has staff available 24/7 to consult
health care providers on risk-status of individuals. They can be contacted by
phone at 402-471-2937 . Refer to link below for more information.
Discussion with Infectious Diseases inpatient attending by phone is highly
recommended. Use the link below to obtain the pager number for on-call staff.
All post-exposure prophylaxis should begin with immediate thorough cleansing of
all wounds with soap and water. After cleansing, use povidine-iodine solution to
Patients without history of rabies vaccination
After wound cleansing, administer rabies immune globulin and first dose of
Administer second, third and fourth doses of rabies vaccine series on days 3, 7,
and 14. An additional dose is given on day 28 for immunocompromised patients.
Patients with history of rabies vaccination
Patients with a history of complete pre-exposure vaccination regimen and a
documented antibody response to the rabies virus, do not require rabies immune
globulin administration. If the patient does not meet these criteria, treat as a
patient without history of rabies vaccination above. If patient does meet these
criteria, after wound cleansing, administer first dose of rabies vaccine series.
Administer second dose of rabies vaccine series on day 3.
In bite wounds that break the skin, tetanus vaccine is indicated if patient has
received <3 doses of tetanus vaccine or immunization history is unknown. Tetanus
immune globulin is also indicated in these patients if they have a tetanus prone
wound. For patients with 3 or more documented tetanus vaccine doses, tetanus
vaccine is indicated if >5 years since last booster in tetanus prone wounds, and
indicated if >10 years since last booster in non-tetanus-prone wounds.

The goal of treatment is control of symptoms, not cure. General treatment

Contents.Text: From 10% to 40% of adults are colonized with Staphylococcus aureus, and the
anterior nares is the most common site of colonization. A majority of people
never have disease with S. aureus, but a tiny fraction of people develop
clinical infections with the S. aureus that has colonized their skin or anterior
nares. Steps to decolonize the skin and anterior nares can transiently diminish
or eradicate S. aureus colonization and can prevent post-operative wound
infection in certain high-risk circumstances. For people who have other forms of
recurrent S. aureus disease, not associated with an operation, results with
decolonization have been disappointing, and decolonization is not routinely
recommended. Colonization typically reappears in most patients within a few days
or weeks after decolonization has been attempted. Clinicians occasionally wish
to attempt decolonization for patients with frequent, troublesome recurrences.
The procedure here is one of several that have been studied, but none have been
particularly effective over the long run.
Consultation with Infectious Diseases is recommended.

Contents.Text: Stasis dermatitis is a common condition that is often confused with
bacterial cellulitis. Stasis dermatitis does not benefit from antimicrobial
therapy. It is important to distinguish between the two. The provider
should be mindful of the fact that bacterial cellulitis can occur on skin
with underlying stasis dermatitis. (See link below for bacterial cellulitis)
Common risk factors for venous stasis include advancing age, family
history of venous disease, increased body mass index, smoking, a history of
trauma, prior venous thrombosis and pregnancy. Chronic venous disease and
arterial vascular disease have some common risk factors (eg, smoking,
obesity) and pathophysiological processes. The most common symptoms reported
by patients with chronic venous disease are limb discomfort (tired, heavy
legs), pain, and limb swelling. Swelling is often worse with prolonged
standing and improves with leg elevation and walking. The skin of the
anterior surfaces of the lower legs often has brown or blue-grey
People with venous stasis are prone to develop stasis dermatitis which
is one of the most common and earliest dermatologic signs of chronic venous
insufficiency. Stasis dermatitis is an inflammatory process that presents as
an eczematous rash characterized by itching, erythema, scaling, weeping,
erosions, and crusting. Longstanding cases may develop lipodermatosclerosis
a fibrosing panniculitis of the subcutaneous tissue. Lipodermatosclerosis
typically starts with a firm area of induration at the medial ankle. As the
process progresses, the entire leg lower leg can become involved with
extension up to the mid leg in more advanced cases. The skin overlying the
panniculitis is typically heavily pigmented and bound down to the
subcutaneous tissues. Brawny edema above the fibrotic area and on the foot
below is seen in advanced cases. Leukocytosis and fever are common in people
Chronic venous disease is the most common cause of leg ulcers. They
are usually found low on the medial ankle over a perforating vein, or along
the course of the great or small saphenous veins. They occur more proximally
if precipitated by trauma. Venous ulcers are not found on the forefoot or
above the level of the knee. Venous ulcers can be multiple or single, and
can be exquisitely tender, shallow, exudative and have a granulation base.
The ulcer borders are usually irregular but not undermined. They can extend
circumferentially around the leg if left untreated.
Arterial ulcers are typically painful, and punched out or stellate. The
surrounding skin is red and taut. Some arterial ulcers are pale - others have
a black or yellow eschar. They are often associated with trauma and commonly
occur on the foot over pressure points. There may be other signs of arterial
insufficiency on the lower limb including thin atrophic or hairless skin,
poor pedal pulses, diminished capillary refill, or hypertrophic deformed
Patients with stasis or lipodermatosclerosis are prone to bouts of
bacterial cellulitis, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus or encapsulated
streptococci. Typically, stasis dermatitis develops slowly, over a week or
more. It is often bilateral. The onset of bacterial cellulitis is usually
abrupt, typically developing over 1 or 2 days. Bacterial cellulitis often
starts in one area and spreads to adjacent areas. Bacterial cellulitis is
unilateral. Both can present with fever and leukocytosis.
In a patient with stasis and cellulitis and the physician is uncertain
about whether bacterial cellulitis is present, the physician should consider
a trial of bed rest, leg elevation, and if there is fluid overload, diuresis
If the cellulitis improves in 24-48 hours, antibacterial therapy and the
attendant adverse reactions can be avoided. If it is clear that bacterial
cellulitis has occurred, antimicrobial therapy should be given.

Contents.Text: Consult Infectious Diseases in all cases. Evaluation and management are complex.
Syphilis is a sexually transmitted disease caused by the spirochete Treponema
pallidum that can manifest as a variety of signs or symptoms. Primary syphilis
typically consists of painless ulcers or chancre at the site of infection with
regional adenopathy. Secondary syphilis often includes a skin rash (disseminated
and/or including the palms and soles), fever, malaise, mucocutaneous lesions and
lymphadenopathy. Tertiary syphilis includes those with cardiovascular or
Latent syphilis is a period of disease when a patient does not have symptoms but
is found to be infected through serologic testing. Early latent syphilis refers
to latent syphilis acquired within the preceding year and late latent syphilis
A presumptive diagnosis is made through use of a nontreponemal or serologic
test (i.e. rapid plasma reagin [RPR]) and a treponemal test (i.e. fluorescent
treponemal antibody absorbed [FTA-ABS]). Direct methods through darkfield
microscopy and direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) must be used for definitive
diagnosis since T. pallidum cannot be cultured.

Contents.Text: Acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) typically presents with fever, dysuria,
chills, malaise, myalgia, pelvic or perianal pain. On exam, the prostate gland

urine culture is positive. Men with dysuria and fever but without pyuria and/or
bacteriuria should be seen by a urologist. If there is any suspicion of abscess,
the patient should be seen by a urologist.
Those with recent urinary tract instrumentation or surgery (e.g., prostate
biopsy, vasectomy) are associated with enteric Gram-negative rods. There are
cases of ABP associated with N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Resistant
organisms are more likely if the patient has been in the hospital for more than
48 hours or received a course of antibiotics. There is increasing resistance in
A midstream urine sample before antibiotics are taken and send for culture and
susceptibility testing should be performed in all patients to guide
antimicrobial therapy. When S. aureus is recovered from a urine
culture, it is important to perform blood cultures to evaluate whether the
bacteriuria reflects seeding of the prostate or urine from bacteremia.
Patients at risk of sexually transmitted infections should be assessed for
Duration of therapy for ABP is usually 2 weeks, although it can be continued for
up to 4 weeks for severe illness or treatment of patients with concomitant
Give oral antibiotics first line if the person can take oral medicines, and the

Contents.Text: Community-acquired bacterial sinusitis is most often due to Streptococcus
pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae or Moraxella catarrhalis. Streptococci,

Treatment for first 10 days of illness
Treat with decongestants, analgesics, and nasal saline spray.
Treatment of cases that have not improved in 10 days despite
treatment with decongestants, analgesics, and nasal saline.
If symptoms worsen despite 72 hours or  fail to improve after 3-5 days of
initial empirical antimicrobial therapy, broaden coverage, switch to different
antimicrobial class and treat 7-10 days. If symptoms continue to worsen or there
is no improvement after 3-5 more days of treatment, obtain CT to investigate
non-infectious or suppurative causes. ENT consultation is recommended. If
sinuses are aspirated, specimens should be cultured.

syncytial virus (RSV). Although response to vaccination with the attenuate
influenza vaccine in patients on chemotherapy is variable, ranging
from 24-75%, immnunoprophylaxis with the influenza vaccine is recommended

endemic, chemoprophylaxis can be considered in addition to vaccination in
exposed patients with a high risk of influenza complications.
Prophylaxis and monitoring for CMV reactivation is not recommended unless

Contents.Text: PREVENTION OF ANTIVIRAL INFECTIONS IN A PATIENT WITH MALIGNANCY
Viral infections reactivate in a small percentage of people with malignancy
Most viral infections in patients with hematologic malignancies or solid
tumors result from reactivation of asymptomatic latent infections,
predominantly of herpes viruses, including herpes simplex virus (HSV),
varicella zoster virus (VZV) and cytomegalovirus (CMV). Exogenous
respiratory tract infections caused by influenza, parainfluenza
or respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are less common.
The main risk factor for clinically relevant reactivation is profound
disruption of cellular immune response, usually due to chemotherapy.
The duration and severity of neutropenia are of lesser importance.
The risk of viral disease increases with the intensity and duration

Solid tumors do not significantly compromise the cellular immune system.
Therefore, patients are at low risk for opportunistic viral infections.
Documented invasive viral infections are very rare. Coincidental
mucocutaneous infections by herpes simplex are easily treated and do not
result in life-threatening invasive infections. Reactivation of
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) or Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is rarely observed.
In patients with acute leukemia, treatment is highly aggressive and consists
of a combination of various cytotoxic agents administered in sequential
cycles as induction, consolidation and maintenance therapy. Persistent, i.e.
>10 days and profound neutropenia (<500 neutrophils) regularly occurs and
correlates with the risk of developing fever and infections. Almost all viral
infections during neutropenia constitute reactivations of herpes viruses.
None of the available studies demonstrated an effect of antiviral prophylaxis
on the initiation of antibiotic treatment, number of febrile days, duration

Contents.Text: APPROACH TO FOOT ULCER WITH INFECTION
Whenever possible, material should be obtained for Gram stain and culture.
Specimens from deep ulcer biopsy, aspiration, or bone biopsy are superior to
wound swab or drainage.  Pathogen identification is especially important because
therapy is often given for weeks.
While foot ulcers in patients with diabetes typically have many bacterial
species on the surface, disease is usually caused by only one or two.  When
Staphylococcus aureus is present in a surface culture, it is usually a pathogen
in the deeper tissues.  Therapy can usually be directed against the predominant
or virulent organisms found on surface cultures and need not be active against
every isolate.  To reduce uncertainty it is better to obtain deeper cultures.
Bacteria that are most likely to be responsible for invasive infection include
S. aureus, streptococci, enteric gram-negative bacilli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa,
and anaerobes typical of the human enteric flora.  When there is no evidence

delivery, and lower birth weight. Screening for bacteriuria is recommended at
least once early in pregnancy. If bacteriuria is not found upon initial testing,
further screening cultures are not needed. If bacteriuria (>10,000 CFU/mL) is
present, the patient should be treated. Testing should be repeated throughout

Contents.Item: ORZID3 NE GMENU BACTERIAL VAGINOSIS MALE SEXUAL PARTNER
Contents.DisplayText: Concurrent Male Partner Treatment for Recurrent, Symptomatic Bacterial Vaginosis

Contents.Text: Vaginitis usually presents with discharge, itching, irritation, odor, or pain.
Bacterial vaginosis is the most common form of vaginitis. Normal hydrogen
peroxide and lactic acid producing vaginal flora, including Lactobacillus
species, is reduced and high concentrations of anaerobic bacterial pathogens are
present. Pathogenic bacteria commonly include Gardnerella vaginalis, Mycoplasma
hominis, Nobiluncus, Prevotella and other Gram-negative anaerobes.
Vaginal pH should be measured, and the specimen should be examined under the
microscope for identification of clue cells (epithelial cell coated with
bacteria). In bacterial vaginosis the vaginal pH is high (> 4.5), the discharge
is homogenous and gray-white, and the specimen has a positive amine or whiff
test characterized by a fishy odor before or after addition of 10% KOH.
Bacterial vaginosis nucleic acid amplification tests are available for common
pathogens to aide in identification of pathogen(s).
Bacterial vaginosis may be transmitted sexually. Patients at risk of sexually
transmitted infections should be assessed for treatment.

Recurrent candida vulvovaginitis is treated as complicated candida

Contents.Text: CHRONIC PROSTATITIS / CHRONIC PELVIC PAIN SYNDROME
Chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CP/CPPS) is a clinical
syndrome in males defined by pain or discomfort in the pelvic region, often
accompanied by urologic symptoms or sexual dysfunction. Despite the use of the
term "prostatitis," it is unclear to what degree the prostate is the source of
Research guidelines define chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome
(CP/CPPS) as chronic pelvic pain for at least three of the preceding six months
in the absence of other identifiable causes, often associated with urinary
This syndrome presents with intermittent perineal and/or low back pain,
obstructive voiding symptoms, relatively normal examination, and negative urine
cultures. In patients who have a negative urine culture and features consistent
with CP/CPPS, antimicrobial therapy is not indicated.
Consult urology for non-antimicrobial therapy recommendations (e.g. alpha-
adrenergic antagonists, anti-inflammatory medications) to reduce symptoms.

Contents.Text: Diagnosis of chronic sinusitis is based on presence of at least 2 of the 4
cardinal signs/symptoms lasting >/= 12 weeks. In addition, diagnosis requires
objective evidence of mucosal inflammation using nasal endoscopy and/or CT
imaging. The initial therapy for chronic sinusitis is treatment with intranasal
corticosteroids and saline. For patients with severe nasal blockage by polyps,
treat with a short course of oral glucocorticoids. Reassess patient after 1 to 3
months of intranasal therapy or after completion of glucocorticoid therapy. If
signs/symptoms have not improved, consult surgery, ENT and Infectious Diseases
Acute exacerbations of chronic sinusitis can be caused by discontinuing medical
therapy, viral infections, allergens, noxious inhalants and bacterial or fungal
infections. Bacterial infections should be suspected when the patient has
increased signs/symptoms persisting for more than 10 days. Refer to Severe
Sinusitis recommendations for choice of antimicrobial therapy in these patients.
Repeated use of the same agent should be avoided to prevent promotion of drug
resistant bacteria or increased fungal colonization.

CAP Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) or PORT Score
The CAP pneumonia severity index is useful for estimation of mortality risk for
a patient with pneumonia.  Pre-estimated risk can then be used to determine how
aggressively to treat the patient's pneumonia and whether the patient can be
treated safely outside of the hospital.
The Community-Acquired Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) is a guide and
should be used to augment clinical judgment. If social circumstances
or cognitive dysfunction would interfere with success of outpatient
treatment, the patient should be hospitalized.
If a patient has taken an antimicrobial in the previous 3 months, it is prudent
to avoid giving the same or a similar drug for the current episode of pneumonia.

Signs and symptoms that may indicate infection has extended beyond the bladder

Contents.Text: Conjunctivitis is associated with viral or bacterial pathogens. Viral
conjunctivitis presents with watery discharge. Bacterial infections are more
likely to present with thick exudate and conjunctival injection. Allergic
conjunctivitis typically presents with stringy mucus. If there is pus
(hypopion), corneal involvement, possible bacterial conjunctivitis, or
Viral conjunctivitis is most commonly caused by adenovirus. It is self-limited
and antivirals provide no benefit. Symptomatic treatment with ophthalmic
antihistamine/decongestants and warm or cool compresses may relieve symptoms.
Bacterial conjunctivitis is most commonly associated with Staphylococcus aureus,
Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus spp., Moraxella catarrhalis,
Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Neisseria spp. or enteric gram-negative rods. It is
generally self-limited, but topical antimicrobials reduce duration of symptoms
and limit person-to-person spread of infection. If symptoms do not improve after
2 days of antimicrobial therapy, the patient should be seen by an

Contents.Text: Epididymitis is inflammation of the epididymis and when testicles are involved
is referred to as epididymo-orchitis. Acute epididymitis is the most common
cause of scrotal pain in adults. Other features include scrotal erythema and
edema, pyuria, dysuria, thickened epididymis, swollen testis, and is usually
unilateral. It is primarily caused by infection but can also result from trauma
and autoimmune diseases. Testicular torsion should be ruled out before
treatment. Most cases in men aged 35 and older, those with recent urinary tract
instrumentation or surgery (e.g., prostate biopsy, vasectomy) are associated
with enteric Gram-negative rods. Most cases in men under age 35 are associated
with N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Resistant organisms are more likely if
the patient has been in the hospital for more than 48 hours or received a course
of antibiotics. There is increasing resistance in urinary pathogens to
A urine analysis, urine culture and urine nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT)
should be performed in all cases of suspected epididymitis before starting
Patients at risk of sexually transmitted infections should be assessed for
treatment. Refer to the Urogenital section of the Antimicrobial CDSS for more
Patients with bacterial epididymitis treated with antibiotics should improve
within two or three days. If no improvement is noted, other causes of scrotal
pain and referral to a urologist should be considered.
Management should include bed rest, analgesics, and scrotal elevation. Older men
should have their residual urinary volume checked. If the residual volume is
elevated, the patient should be seen by a urologist as epididymitis is unlikely
to respond if the prostate is blocking the vas deferens.
Patients at risk of sexually transmitted infections should be assessed for

Contents.Text: Fever of unknown origin (FUO) is the occurrence of several episodes of fever
greater than 101 degrees Fahrenheit over a period of at least 3 weeks despite 1
week of hospital evaluation. Cases with FUO are often classified in four
categories: (1) classical, (2) neutropenic, (3) nosocomial, and (4) fever in
persons with HIV/AIDS. Empirical antimicrobial therapy is rarely indicated in
Note that FUO in neutropenic patients refers to persistent fever that has
remained undiagnosed after extensive diagnostic work and empirical antimicrobial
therapy. New fever in patients with profound neutropenia is a different syndrome
and does require empirical antimicrobial therapy. Infectious Diseases should be
involved in any case where empirical treatment for fever of unknown origin is
being considered. For more information refer to the neutropenic fever

Contents.Text: Several types of neurological dysfunction predispose patients to infectious
diseases.  Comatose patients are unable to keep weight off dependent tissues,
predisposing them to decubitus ulcers and pressure necrosis.  Atelectasis is
common in obtunded patients who cannot cough or breathe deeply.  When patients
require artificial ventilation, intubation compounds the risk of respiratory
Neurological dysfunction of the bladder can interfere with normal bladder
emptying and predisposes patients to bacteriuria.  The risk of bacteruria
increases if patients are catheterized.  Antimicrobial treatment is not
indicated for asymptomatic bacteriuria.  It provides no benefit and increases
risk of colonization with resistant organisms.
Neurological dysfunction of the gastrointestinal or pulmonary systems
predisposes patients to aspiration of oropharyngeal or gastric contents.
Aspiration causes fever, inflammation, and/or pulmonary infiltrate, but does not
require antimicrobial treatment. Bacterial pneumonia occurs in a minority of
patients who experience significant aspiration, typically about 3 days later.
The patient usually improves for the first 2 days and then worsens as bacterial
pneumonia develops with increased fever, new or progressive infiltrates,

When asplenic patients present with fever or other symptoms suggesting systemic

Contents.Text: Impetigo is a superficial skin infection that rarely causes systemic
symptoms. Ecthyma is a skin infection characterized by crusted sores
beneath which ulcers form. It is a deep form of impetigo, as the same
bacteria causing the infection are involved. Ecthyma causes deeper
erosions of the skin into the dermis.
Gram stain and culture of the pus or exudates from skin lesions of
impetigo and ecthyma are recommended to help identify whether
Staphylococcus aureus and/or beta-hemolytic Streptococcus is the cause.
Bullous and non-bullous impetigo can be treated with oral or topical

bodies, or allergies. About half of cases of infectious keratitis are caused by

gram-negative bacilli. Viruses are the second leading cause. Fungi and parasites
have also been associated with corneal infection. Obtain corneal scrapings for
gram stain and bacterial and viral cultures and start empirical therapy

scraping and give empirical antibacterial drops immediately. Modify therapy
based on Ophthalmology and/or Infectious Diseases recommendations. Ophthalmic
corticosteroids are contraindicated in patients with keratitis.

Contents.Text: Pulmonary and/or Infectious Diseases consultations are strongly encouraged for
all cases.  Obtain samples for gram stain and culture from fine needle
aspiration whenever possible.  Sputum culture is less helpful because it will be
contaminated with upper respiratory flora.  Classically, lung abscess is a
complication of mixed anaerobic and aerobic pulmonary infection. The initial
infection may or may not be clinically apparent.  Malaise, weight loss, fever,
chills, and malodorous sputum typically develop over a period of weeks.
Cavitation and/or abscess can occur in cases of pneumonia from a single
pathogen, commonly Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Antimicrobial treatment should be directed against the specific pathogen.
Treat for 6 to 8 weeks and adjust treatment based on clinical response.  Oral
medications should be used in patients who can take them.

Contents.Text: LYME DISEASE AND OTHER TICK-BORNE ILLNESSES
Patients who display signs of illness or fever within 30 days of removing an
attached tick should be evaluated for tick-borne illness. In the upper Midwest
these are Lyme, anaplasmosis, babesiosis, ehrlichiosis, and Powassan virus
disease. Patients who have been bitten by an Ixodes spp. tick (deer tick) but
who do not display signs or symptoms of infection should not be treated with
antimicrobials. Refer to recommendations below for pathogen specific
Powassan virus disease - contact Infectious Diseases for more Information.
Lyme disease results from the transmission of Borrelia burgdorferi from an
Ixodes spp. tick bite. Prophylactic antimicrobial treatment may be beneficial in
certain patients who have been bitten while in endemic areas.
Except for erythema migrans, Lyme disease is a complicated, difficult disease to
diagnose and treat. Infectious Diseases consultation is strongly encouraged.

Contents.Text: Patients who have been bitten while in endemic areas of New England, Mid-
Atlantic States, Minnesota, and Wisconsin where local rate of Ixodes spp. tick
infection rate with Borrelia burgdorferi in an endemic area may be treated with
prophylactic antibiotics for prevention of Lyme disease. Using a wait and see
method by monitoring for signs and symptoms of Lyme disease is also an
acceptable approach in patients who have been bitten by an Ixodes spp. tick.
All following criteria must be met to be considered for prophylactic treatment
1. Doxycycline is not contraindicated (i.e. allergy, pregnant, lactating)

Contents.Text: ERYTHEMA MIGRANS ASSOCIATED WITH LYME DISEASE
For pregnant patients or those with contraindications to doxycycline:
Erythema migrans is the first manifestation of Lyme disease in 70-80% of cases.
It is typically an erythematous circular rash, 5cm or larger in diameter, with
induration and central clearing (although other patterns occur). It usually
develops at the site of the bite and/or in one or more distant locations. The
rash occurs 3 to 30 days after the bite. Rashes with onset less than 3 days
after a tick bite are not from Lyme disease.

Contents.Text: Acute mastoiditis most commonly occurs as a suppurative complication of acute
otitis media. Diagnosis is supported by CT or MRI imaging and culture of
drainage. Antibiotics and drainage of middle ear are sufficient treatment in
most cases. Mastoidectomy is necessary if abscess has formed in the mastoid
bone. If complication of first episode of acute otitis media, etiologies
typically include Streptococcus pneumonia (most common), Streptococcus pyogenes,
or Staphylococcus aureus. If secondary to chronic otitis media, etiologies
typically include Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Patients
usually too ill for outpatient therapy. ENT consultation recommended. Obtain
cultures of auditory canal or middle ear fluid (preferred).
Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for parenteral therapy
Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for parenteral therapy
Step down treatment after initial intravenous antibiotic treatment in patients
who can tolerate oral therapy. Base selection on culture results. Adjust for a
total duration of 3 weeks of antimicrobial therapy.
Chronic mastoiditis is usually the result of chronic otitis media with
perforation of the tympanic membrane. There is often associated formation of a
cholesteatoma (keratoma). Diagnosis is supported by CT or MRI imaging and
culture of drainage. Long term treatment with topical antimicrobials is first
line therapy. Infection is often polymicrobial, including Staphylococcus aureus,
Pseudomonas aeruginosa and anaerobes. Treatment should be managed in
collaboration with otolaryngology and includes topical antimicrobials, care of
external auditory canal, and is some cases mastoidectomy. If possible, withhold
therapy until a pathogen is identified by culture of drainage to direct therapy.
Specific drug choice dictated by culture results.

MORE ABOUT PHARYNGITIS/ TONSILLITIS AND THE MODIFIED CENTOR SCORE
As most cases are of viral origin, antimicrobials are not indicated in these
cases. Warm saltwater gargle rinses and throat lozenges provide temporary relief
of throat pain. Five to 10% of cases are caused by group A Streptococcus.
Antimicrobial treatment reduces symptoms by one day, prevents suppurative
complications and prevents acute rheumatic fever, an uncommon disease in US
Streptococcal pharyngitis or tonsillitis should be suspected when patients have
fever and exudate on the pharyngeal wall or tonsils without symptoms like cough,
nasal congestion, or runny nose that suggest viral infection or common cold. If
streptococcal pharyngitis is suspected in adults, perform PCR testing for group
A streptococci and treat only if positive.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a rare cause of pharyngitis. N. gonorrhoeae should be
considered for patients with risk factors for sexually transmitted diseases. N.
gonorrhoeae infections must be reported to the state health department and this
will be done by Infection Control if the culture is positive.

Since infection can be rapidly progressive and severe, broad-spectrum

Candidates for empirical treatment with oral antimicrobials include those who

Contents.Item: ORZID3 NE GMENU ABX STEP DOWN TREATMENT

Contents.Text: Antimicrobials are not indicated for uncomplicated pancreatitis.
In cases of necrotizing pancreatitis without infection, antimicrobial
prophylaxis does not improve patient outcomes. Antimicrobials increase the risk
of fungal superinfection and should not be used.
Antimicrobials are indicated for cases with pancreatic abscess, infected
pancreatic pseudocyst, or infected necrotic pancreas (phlegmon). The diagnosis
of infection can be difficult and may require aspiration. Consultation with
Gastroenterology and/or Infectious Diseases is encouraged.
Pancreatic abscess, infected pancreatic pseudocyst, or infected necrotic
Total duration of antimicrobial therapy is typically 2 to 4 weeks
Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS

female reproductive tract.  Likely bacterial pathogens include Neisseria
gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, anaerobes, enteric Gram-negative rods, and
Streptococcus agalactiae.  PID should be considered in sexually active women
with pelvic tenderness and signs of lower genital tract inflammation.  Signs and
symptoms may be mild or non-specific, and providers should have a low threshold
to initiate treatment. All women who are diagnosed with acute PID should be
tested for N. gonorrohoeae, C. trachomatis, and HIV. Male sex partners of
patients with PID should be examined and treated (see below) if they had sexual
contact within the 60 days before onset of the patient's symptoms.

Contents.Text: Periodontal disease, including gingivitis and periodontitis, may progress into
more severe disease or cause hematogenous spreading of bacteria if left
untreated. All patients with periodontal disease should be referred to the
dental service for assessment and direction of treatment. In the presence of
gingivitis, the most commonly isolated subgingival flora includes Prevotella
intermedia, Capnocytophaga spp, Finegoldia magna and Peptostreptococcus. In the
presence of periodontitis, flora increases in complexity to most commonly
include Porphyromonas gingivalis, P. intermedia, Aggregatibacter
actinomycetemcomitans, Tanneralla forsythensis and Treponema denticola.

Contents.Text: Diagnosis and treatment are complex, consult Infectious Diseases in all cases.
Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly termed Pneumocystis carinii) in an ubiquitious
organism that causes disease in people with compromised cell-mediated immunity.
Disease is exceedingly rare in people with intact host defenses. Pneumonia is
the usual manifestation but P. jirovecii can infect extrapulmonary sites,
especially in patients who have been receiving prophylaxis with aerosolized
pentanmidine. P. jirovecii disease occurs most commonly in people with AIDS and
The abbreviation PCP is often used for Pneumocystis pneumonia. It was derived
from the old species name, Pneumocystis carinii.
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMZ) is the treatment of choice for P.
jirovecii disease, including disease that occurs despite TMP-SMZ prophylaxis.
Corticosteriods should be prescribed for patients with AIDS and P. jirovecii
pneumonia and an arterial oxygen tension <70 torr or an alveolar-arterial oxygen

Contents.Text: Indications for primary prophylaxis of P. jirovecii include:
1) HIV/AIDS patients with CD4 count <200 cells/microliter
2) Hematopoietic or organ transplantation patients during immunosuppression
3) Patients receiving Alemtuzumab, temozolomide or fludarabine
4) Patients receiving >/= 20mg equivalent of prednisone per day for over 1 month
5) Patients with acute lymphocytic leukemia, rheumatologic disease receiving
immunosuppressive therapy and certain primary immunodeficiencies (e.g. severe
combined immunodeficiency, idiopathic CD4 T-lymphocytopenia, hyper-IgM syndrome)
Dose and duration of prophylaxis varies with the indication. Please contact
Infectious Diseases or Hematology/Oncology for more information.
Prophylaxis should be discontinued when host defenses are restored. In persons
with AIDS on highly active antiretroviral therapy, Prophylaxis should be
discontinued when the CD4 cell concentrations remain over 200 cells/microliter
for 3-6 months in patients, except that prophylaxis should be continued for
life in those who have had P. jirovecii disease.

Antifungal chemoprophylaxis is often given to patients undergoing induction
chemotherapy for acute leukemia expected to have profound neutropenia (less than
100 neutrophils and bands per milliliter) for more than 10 days and for patients
receiving allogeneic stem cell transplantation.  For most other patients the
expected benefits do not outweigh the risks of adverse effects and selection of
Antifungal is usually given until the absolute neutrophil concentration
increases to more than 500 cells/microliter in patients undergoing induction
chemotherapy for leukemia.  Duration is 100 days for patients undergoing stem
cell transplantation.  Some physicians continue prevention after 100 days if
corticosteroids are part of the immunosuppressive regimen.
Recommend posaconazole prophylaxis for patients with Acute Myeloid Leukemia.

Contents.Item: ORZID2 NE GMENU ABX REFERENCES

Contents.Text: Bacteremia occurs several times a day during the course of daily activities like
eating and brushing teeth and rarely results in endocarditis, even in people
with abnormal valves.  While bacteremia might occur following dental or other
procedures, most cases of endocarditis are from the millions more episodes of
transient bactermia a person experiences per year from ordinary daily
activities.  There is no evidence that antimicrobial prophylaxis prevents
endocarditis after procedures.  The best available evidence suggests that
prophylactic antimicrobials confer more risks than benefits in most situations.
A decision about whether to administer antimicrobial prophylaxis should be based
on both the risk of endocarditis conferred by the patient's cardiac defect and
the risk of bacteremia from a planned dental or surgical procedure.
For complete information, follow this link:

Step 1.  Assess the risk of endocarditis for your patient

>>  Certain specific congenital heart conditions - refer to the full guidelines
(link above) or consult Cardiology for more detailed recommendations
>>  Cardiac transplant that develops a problem in the heart valve
Note: prophylaxis is NO LONGER RECOMMENDED for patients with:
>>  Congenital heart conditions such as ventricular septal defect, atrial
Step 2.  Assess the risk of bacteremia from the planned procedure
>>  All dental procedures that involve manipulation of gingival tissue or the
periapical region of teeth or perforation of the oral mucosa.
>>  Procedures on the respiratory tract that involve incision or biopsy of the
respiratory mucosa, such as tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy.
>>  Prophylaxis is recommended for bronchoscopy when procedure involves incision
>>  Procedures that involve incision through infected skin, skin structures, or
>>  Dermatologic procedures that breach the oral mucosa.

place) of infection from hematogenous seeding.  The risk of joint infection
after dental or surgical procedures is exceedingly small.  Existing data do not
support the use of prophylactic antimicrobial prophylaxis for patients with
prosthetic joints undergoing procedures.  Since the overall risk of prosthesis
infection is slightly higher during the first 2 years after implantation, some

Contents.Text: REACTIVATION OF PRIMARY INFECTION (ZOSTER OR SHINGLES)
Zoster represents reactivation of varicella-zoster virus. After primary
infection, virus remains latent in the sensory dorsal root ganglia.
Reactivation syndrome is characterized by painful, unilateral, vesicular,
Vaccinate all adults greater than or equal to 50 years of age with the
recombinant zoster vaccine regardless of past episode or receipt of the live
Give recombinant zoster vaccine x2, 2nd dose 2-6 months after the first
Treatment is not beneficial, none is recommended.
Treatment with antivirals can shorten duration of pain and rash in patients over
50 years old. Treatment must be started within 72 hours of onset.
There is evidence that addition of corticosteroids to antiviral
therapy decreases pain and duration of rash and improves quality of life
modestly during the acute shingles episode. Corticosteroids do not decrease the
incidence of post-herpetic neuralgia. Some authorities recommend addition of
corticosteroid therapy to antiviral therapy for patients over age 50 years.
Corticosteroids are not recommended for patients at greater risk for steroid
toxicities (e.g., insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, hypertension, peptic
ulcer disease) or for immunocompromised patients.
Immunocompromised patients at increased risk for complications of VZV disease
include: patients with malignancy, current immunosuppressive therapy, or HIV
infection. Treatment with antivirals shortens duration of symptoms and reduces
incidence of complications. In immunocompromised patients, treatment is
recommended to be started at any point during an active infection.

Contents.Text: Retinitis is a subset of uveitis, is rare in immunocompetent people: in these
individuals it is usually caused by varicella-zoster virus (VZV) or herpes
simplex virus (HSV). Retinitis is more common in immunocompromised patients and
cytomegalovirus being the most common pathogen in these patients. Other
retinitis pathogens include Toxoplasma gondii, Bartonella henselae, Histoplasma
capsulatum, and Treponema pallidum. In most cases, patients have other
neurological symptoms or signs.  Patients with candidemia may present with 1-3
mm white punctate retinal lesions called cotton-wool spots. These may only be
visible on fundus examination. Treatment of candidal retinitis  is systemic
antifungal therapy. Consult Ophthalmology, Infectious Diseases, or Neurology for
VZV and HSV cause nearly all cases of acute retinal necrosis (ARN), with a small
number being caused by cytomegalovirus. ARN is a rapidly progressing retinitis
that occurs primarily in immunocompetent people and can cause vision loss.

Contents.Text: Scabies is an infestation of the skin by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei.
It is transmitted by skin to skin contact. Outbreaks occur in nursing
homes, day care centers, and residential institutions.  Scabies is highly
contagious and meticulous infection control is needed.
Treatment is a single application of permethrin cream.  Some experts recommend
a second application 7-10 days after the first application if the patient is
still symptomatic or if live mites are found at that time.  Contact Dermatology
or Infectious Diseases for more information.
Treat family members and other close contacts to prevent spread and recurrence.
Repeat application 7-10 days after the first application if patient is still

Contents.Text: SECOND RECURRENCE OF CLOSTRIDIOIDES DIFFICILE INFECTION (CDI)
Discontinue implicated antibiotic(s). Narrow antibiotic spectrum if antibiotic
therapy is still needed. Avoid antiperistaltic agents (narcotics, loperamide,
etc.). Avoid antacid therapy without clear indication. If diarrhea has improved
or resolved prior to starting C. difficile treatment, consider re-assessing the
diagnosis before initiating therapy. C. difficile infection usually responds to
antimicrobial therapy. If symptoms do not respond to appropriate antimicrobial
(Vancomycin 125 mg PO q6h for 10 days, then taper and pulse with 125 mg po q12h
for 7 days, then 125mg po qday for 7 days, then 125mg every other day for 6
(Fidaxomicin 200mg po bid x5days,then 200mg every other day x20days)
Third or more recurrence: Consult Gastroenterology or Infectious Disease

Contents.Text: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) presents with severe skin
blistering and exfoliation resulting from toxins produced by Staphylococcus
aureus.  SSSS is usually found in children and rarely in older adults.  Obtain
a skin biopsy to differentiate between SSSS and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Initiate anti-staphylococcal therapy and obtain cultures and susceptibilities.
If cultures reveal methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), change
to nafcillin or cefazolin for better antimicrobial activity.

Contents.Text: CARDIAC SURGERY AND IMPLANTATION OF PACEMAKER
Antimicrobial prophylaxis is not indicated before cardiac catheterization.
No evidence supports the use of post-operative prophylactic antimicrobials.
However, due to the potentially devastating consequences of sternal wound
infection, expert opinion supports use of a limited number of post-operative
doses.  Discontinue antimicrobials by 48 hours after the procedure, regardless
of the presence of postoperative drains or tubes.
Cefazolin is preferred for prophylaxis, as it is more active than vancomycin
against susceptible staphylococci.  Vancomycin should be used when methicillin-
resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection is likely.  Consult Cardiothoracic
Surgery or Infectious Diseases for more information.
If vancomycin is used give 1000 mg to patients weighing less than 100 kg.  Give
1500 mg if the patient weights 100 or more kg.

Contents.Text: Indications for primary prophylaxis of P. jirovecii include:
1) HIV/AIDS patients with CD4 count <200 cells/microliter
2) Hematopoietic or organ transplantation patients during immunosuppression
3) Patients receiving Alemtuzumab, temozolomide or fludarabine
4) Patients receiving >/= 20mg equivalent of prednisone per day for over 1 month
5) Patients with acute lymphocytic leukemia, rheumatologic disease receiving
immunosuppressive therapy and certain primary immunodeficiencies (e.g. severe
combined immunodeficiency, idiopathic CD4 T-lymphocytopenia, hyper-IgM syndrome)
Dose and duration of prophylaxis varies with the indication. Please contact
Infectious Diseases or Hematology/Oncology for more information.
Prophylaxis should be discontinued when host defenses are restored. In persons
with AIDS on highly active antiretroviral therapy, Prophylaxis should be
discontinued when the CD4 cell concentrations remain over 200 cells/microliter
for 3 months in patients, except that prophylaxis should be continued for life
in those who have had P. jirovecii disease.

Contents.Text: Consult Infectious Diseases in all cases. Evaluation and management are complex.
Syphilis is a sexually transmitted disease caused by the spirochete Treponema
pallidum that can manifest as a variety of signs or symptoms. Primary syphilis
typically consists of painless ulcers or chancre at the site of infection with
regional adenopathy. Secondary syphilis often includes a skin rash (disseminated
and/or including the palms and soles), fever, malaise, mucocutaneous lesions and
lymphadenopathy. Tertiary syphilis includes those with cardiovascular or
Latent syphilis is a period of disease when a patient does not have symptoms but
is found to be infected through serologic testing. Early latent syphilis refers
to latent syphilis acquired within the preceding year and late latent syphilis
refers to all other cases of latent syphilis. Neurosyphilis, Ocular syphilis or
Otosyphilis, can occur at any stage of syphilis with early manifestations (e.g.
meningitis, stroke, vision or hearing loss) occurring within the first months to
years of infection and late manifestations (e.g. dementia, tabes dorsalis)
A presumptive diagnosis is made through use of a nontreponemal or serologic test
(i.e. rapid plasma reagin [RPR]) and a treponemal test (i.e. fluorescent
treponemal antibody absorbed [FTA-ABS]). Direct methods through darkfield
microscopy and direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) must be used for definitive
diagnosis since T. pallidum cannot be cultured.
Persons with sexual contact with a person with primary, secondary or early
latent syphilis within the last 90 days should be presumptively treated even if

URETHRITIS ASSOCIATED WITH SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED DISEASES
The main differential in a person who presents with dysuria is between cystitis
and urethritis. Bacterial urethritis is more likely in people with mild
dysuria, onset over a few days, or recent sexual contact.
The two most common sexually transmitted urethritis pathogens are Neisseria
gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. Nucleic acid amplification tests for
these pathogens are more sensitive than culture and should be used for patients
at risk for sexually transmitted urethritis.

Contents.Text: Cystitis refers to infection of the urinary bladder, but inflammation often
extends into the urethra. Typical symptoms and signs include dysuria, increased
urinary frequency, urgency, and/or suprapubic tenderness.
Most cases of uncomplicated cystitis occur in pre-menopausal, non-pregnant,
Most cases of complicated cystitis are associated with Escherichia coli, but
more resistant pathogens occur, including the Gram-positive pathogens
staphylococci and enterococci. Urine culture should be obtained before
Cystitis is considered complicated when one or more of the following is present
> Structural abnormalities (e.g. presence of obstruction, catheter or
> Metabolic abnormalities that reduce local host defenses (e.g. diabetes,
> Treatment failure or relapse or recurrence of infection
When a patient presents with symptoms of cystitis, urinalysis should be
performed to check for the presence of white blood cells. Increased numbers of
leukocytes (usually >25) in the presence of cystitis symptoms indicates
inflammation and thus cystitis. The bacterial etiology is so predictable that
urine culture is unnecessary and empirical treatment is indicated. The
clinical significance of pyuria in the absence of cystitis symptoms is unclear.
Antimicrobial therapy is not indicated for pyuria in the absence of symptoms.

should determine the INR more frequently than usual and adjust dosage
accordingly. Instruct patients to inform their primary warfarin
provider whenever an antimicrobial is prescribed for them.
